en: The King said:
O Brahmana, the Blessed Lord is himself equal toward all beings, dear to them, and their well-wisher;
how then did he slay the Daityas for the sake of Indra like one who is partial?
"For the sake of this Lord, whose very nature is the supreme good, there is no purpose served by the hosts of gods;
nor does he have any hatred toward the asuras, for he is free from the material qualities (guṇas). Thus it is regarding the qualities of Nārāyaṇa, O most fortunate one."
"A very great doubt has arisen; you ought to dispel it.
The venerable Ṛṣi said:
"Well asked, O Great King, regarding the wonderful life of Hari."

Having bowed to the sage Kṛṣṇa, I shall relate the story of Hari— the greatness of the *Bhāgavata*, which increases devotion to the Lord, is supremely meritorious, and is sung by sages such as Nārada.
For although the Blessed Lord is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), unborn, unmanifest, and beyond material nature (*prakṛti*),
He enters into the qualities of His own *māyā* and thus assumes the state of the oppressed and the oppressor.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of *prakṛti*, not of the Self (*ātman*).
O King, there was neither simultaneous decline nor increase for them; rather,
at the time of the predominance of *sattva*, he favored the gods and sages, at that of *rajas*, the asuras,
and at that of *tamas*, the yakṣas and rākṣasas, according to the conditions of those respective times.
Like light and other elements, he appears as if inseparable from the aggregate of matter and is not distinguished from it;
yet, by churning within themselves, the wise finally perceive the Self abiding in the self.
When He, the Supreme, desiring to create bodies for Himself, emits the quality of passion (rajas) separately through His own creative power (māyā).
O King, when that Lord, desiring to sport amidst the manifold manifestations of *sattva*, is about to lie down to sleep, He impels *tamas*.

O ruler of men, the Lord, the author of truth, creates Time as the moving substratum for both *pradhāna* and the individual soul. O King, this very Time, being the controller, therefore causes *sattva* to flourish, just as it does for the host of gods.
The one of vast renown, beloved by the gods, destroys the Asuras who are hostile to Him and characterized by passion and ignorance.
In this very regard, O King, an ancient history was previously recounted with affection by the celestial sage to Ajātaśatru, who had questioned him during a great sacrifice.
Having witnessed that great wonder at the great Rājasūya sacrifice—
that the King of Cedi had attained *sāyujya* with the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva—
the King, son of Pāṇḍu, [beheld] the celestial Ṛṣi seated there at the ritual.
With a mind struck with wonder, he questioned this while the sages were listening.
Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Oh, how truly marvelous is this, which is difficult even for those who are exclusively devoted to the One to attain!"
O sage, we all desire to know how the attainment of Vāsudeva, the Supreme Reality, came about for the enemy Caidya;
O Blessed One, by the censure of the twice-born, Vena was cast into darkness.
The wicked son of Damaghoṣa, who had been insolent since his childhood, and the evil-minded Dantavakra, both being now filled with resentment toward Govinda,
repeatedly cursed Viṣṇu— that supreme, immutable Brahman.
The white leprosy was not born upon his tongue, nor did the darkness of blindness enter it.
How could those two swiftly meet their dissolution while all the worlds were looking on— that Blessed One whose nature is so difficult to grasp?
"My intellect wanders like the flame of a lamp in the wind;
please explain this most wonderful thing, for you, O Blessed One, are surely the cause of its understanding.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having heard those words of the king, the blessed sage Nārada was pleased; addressing him while the assembly listened to his discourse, he spoke.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, this body is imagined through lack of discrimination by the two— the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa— for the sake of censure, praise, honor,
and insult; just as violence arises from the pride of identifying with it, so too do harshness of speech and punishment.
O King, the inequality among living beings here—this conceit consisting of "mine" and "I"—is what constitutes their bondage; the killing of such beings is true slaughter.
But for Him, the Self of all, there is no such conceit because of His absolute oneness.
For how could violence ever be attributed to Him, the Supreme Controller who disciplines all?

Therefore, whether through the persistence of enmity, or without enmity, or out of fear, or out of affection, or even out of desire—one should engage with Him; for He does not look upon anyone as separate from Himself.
It is my firm conviction that a mortal does not attain such absorption in Me through the yoga of devotion as he does through the persistence of enmity; for example,
a worm confined within a wall by a silkworm caterpillar, while constantly remembering it, [attains its state].

Through the application of fury and fear, one attains His very nature; likewise, those whose sins were purified by enmity toward Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord who had assumed a human form through Māyā, attained Him by constant meditation upon Him.
"Out of desire, hatred, fear, or affection, many have fixed their minds upon the Lord through devotion; having abandoned their sins, they have attained His state.
The cowherd women [attained it] out of desire, Kaṃsa out of fear, and the kings headed by Śiśupāla out of hatred."

"O Lord, because of our kinship with the Vṛṣṇis, we have affection for you; yet through devotion, even one among the five elements would not be indifferent toward the Supreme Person. Therefore, by whatever means possible, one should fix the mind upon Kṛṣṇa."
O Pāṇḍava, Vaśa, the son of his mother’s sister, and Dantavakra were both foremost attendants of Viṣṇu who fell from their positions due to the curse of a brahmin. Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What kind of curse was it, and whose, that would touch the servants of Hari?
The fate of those who are single-mindedly devoted to Hari seems almost incredible,
for they are inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha, devoid of body, senses, and life-breath.
"You ought to explain this connection with the body.
Śrī Nārada said:
"Once, the sons of Brahmā went to the world of Viṣṇu by chance."
Sanandana and the others, who were the ancestors even of the ancients, were wandering through the three worlds with the luster of children five or six years old;
thinking them to be naked infants, the two gatekeepers tried to stop them.

Thus they cursed them in their anger: "O fools, you two do not deserve to dwell at the feet of the Enemy of Madhu, which are free from passion and ignorance; go quickly to the most sinful womb of the Asuras."
Thus cursed, as they were falling from their own abode, they were addressed by the compassionate ones: "May you two be fit for the worlds through three births.
They were born as the two sons of Diti, honored by the Daityas and Dānavas.
Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder brother, and Hiraṇyākṣa was his younger brother;
Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by Hari in the form of a lion,
and Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by Him who assumed the body of a boar for the upholding of the earth.

Hiraṇyakaśipu, desiring to kill his son Prahlāda— who was dear to Keśava— inflicted various tortures upon him for the sake of his death. Yet he [Prahlāda] remained peaceful, viewing all beings as the self and perceiving them with equanimity.
Touched by the splendor of the Lord, he was unable to uproot it despite his efforts.
Thereafter, those two Rākṣasas were born of Keśinī as the sons of Viśravas—
Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa— who caused affliction to all the worlds.
Even there, having become Rāghava, he slew [the demons] for the sake of liberation from the curse;
O Lord, you shall hear of Rāma’s prowess from the mouth of Mārkaṇḍeya. In the meantime, those two have been born here as Kṣatriyas, the sons of your maternal aunt.

Now, freed from the curse and their sins destroyed by the discus of Kṛṣṇa, those two attendants of Viṣṇu were led by Acyuta to the state of being his very self through intense meditation characterized by a persistent bond of enmity; thus they returned once more to the side of Hari.
Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How did enmity arise toward his beloved son, that great-souled one? Tell me, O Blessed One, how Prahlāda attained the nature of Acyuta."
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, when his brother had thus been slain by Hari in the form of a boar,
Hiraṇyakaśipu was consumed with rage and grief.
Filled with rage, biting his lips, and looking toward the smoke-colored sky with eyes blazing with anger, he spoke these words;
his face was made hideous by a frown, and his fierce gaze was marked by formidable fangs.
Raising his trident in the assembly, he spoke thus to the Dānavas:
"O Dānavas, Daityas, Dvimūrdhan, Tryakṣa, Śambara,
Śatabāhu, Hayagrīva, Namuci, Pāka, and Ilvala!"
"O Vipracitti, Puloman, Śakuni, and all the others, listen to my words immediately; let it be done quickly, without delay. My beloved brother and friend has been slain by mean enemies."
Even though Hari was his rear-guard ally,

that compassionate dweller of the forest, having abandoned his true nature, pursued him through various stratagems— just as one might deal with a child of unsteady mind who betrays even those who have shown him affection.

"Once my brother's neck has been pierced by my trident, I, freed from all distress, shall indeed satiate my blood-loving brother with his abundant blood. When that treacherous enemy has been destroyed on that peak, like a tree cut at its roots."
The gods, whose life-breath is Viṣṇu, are withering like trees;
therefore, go now to the earth, which is nourished by the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas,
and destroy those who perform austerities, sacrifices, Vedic study, vows, and acts of charity.
Viṣṇu is the personification of sacrifice, rooted in the rites of the twice-born and consisting of dharma; He is the ultimate refuge of the gods, sages, ancestors, living beings, and dharma itself.
Wherever there are the twice-born, cows, the Vedas, and the duties of the social orders and stages of life—there He resides.
"Go to each and every region and set it ablaze;
tear it down! Taking their master’s command upon their heads with reverence, those who delighted in slaughter carried out the destruction of the people accordingly.
They burned cities, villages, cow-pens, gardens, fields, groves, hermitages, mines, hamlets, market towns,
cow-stations, and fortified settlements. Some tore apart embankments, walls, and gate-towers with spades.

Some, with axes in hand, cut down the trees that provided sustenance; others set fire to the dwellings of the people with blazing torches. Thus was the world repeatedly harassed by the followers of the lords of the Daityas.
The gods, having abandoned heaven, wandered upon the earth unobserved. Hiraṇyakaśipu, distressed by the death of his brother,
performed the funeral rites such as the offering of water and the preparation of the funeral pyre, and then consoled his brother’s sons.
With his speech, he addressed Śakuni, Śambara, Dhṛṣṭi, Bhūtasantāpana, Vṛka,
Kālanābha, Mahānābha, Hariśmaśru, and Utkaca,
as well as their mother Ruṣābhānu and his own mother Diti.
Knowing the proper place and time, the lord of men spoke these gentle words;
Śrī Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O mother, O mother! O daughter-in-law, O sons, you ought not to grieve for the hero."
For heroes, death facing the enemy is praiseworthy and desired;
O lady of virtuous vows, the dwelling of living beings here is like that at a water-station,
brought together in one place by destiny and raised up by their own past actions.
The eternal, immutable, pure, all-pervading, omniscient,
and supreme Self assumes its own subtle body by manifesting the modes of nature through His illusory power (māyā),
just as trees appear to move when the water [upon which they stand] is flowing.
When the eye is whirled around, the earth appears as if it were moving; in the same way,
O blessed lady, when the mind is whirled around by the *guṇas*,
the unchanging person attains the state of identity with them, appearing as if possessed of marks though he is without marks.
This is indeed the inversion of the self: the conception of a mark where there is no mark.
This is union with the pleasant and unpleasant, separation from them, and the cycle of karma;
it is known as birth, destruction, and manifold grief.
Lack of discrimination, anxiety, and the failure to remember the truth— regarding this very matter, they cite this ancient history;
listen to that dialogue between Yama and the kinsmen of the deceased.
Among the Uśīnaras there was a king renowned as Suyajña;
slain in battle by his rivals, his kinsmen attended upon him as he lay there with his jeweled armor shattered and his ornaments and garlands fallen away.
In the battle, he lay with his heart pierced by an arrow, drenched in blood,
with disheveled hair, his eyes destroyed, his lips bitten in fury,
the lotus of his face obscured by dust, and his weapons and arms severed.
Seeing their husband, the lord of Uśīnara, thus treated according to the ritual, the queens were overcome with grief;
crying out, "We are ruined, O our protector! they repeatedly struck their breasts with their hands and fell at his feet.
Weeping loudly, they drenched the lotus-feet of their beloved with tears reddened by the saffron from their breasts.
With their hair and ornaments disheveled, they lamented with wailing cries, producing grief among men:
"Alas! By a pitiless Creator, O Lord, you have been brought to a state beyond our sight.
You who were formerly the provider of livelihood for the Uśīnaras, by him you have now been made the increaser of our sorrows."

"O lord of the earth, how shall we exist without you, our most excellent friend, who are so grateful? O hero, grant us permission to follow upon your footsteps as we serve at your feet, wherever you shall go.
Thus they lamented, having taken hold of their deceased husband.
While they were unwilling to let her body be carried away, the sun set;
there, having heard the lamentations of the kinsmen of the deceased,
Yama himself approached them in the form of a child and spoke.
Śrī Yama said:
"Oh, how great is the delusion of these men, who are advanced in age and yet observe the ways of the world!
Even though they themselves follow the same dharma, they vainly grieve for a mortal who has departed to that very place from which he came."
"Oh, how most blessed we are that, though abandoned here by our parents, we do not feel anxiety;
for he who protects us while we are helpless and being devoured by wolves and other beasts—
he indeed protects us, he who is the imperishable Lord who creates this world by his will, and who both preserves and withdraws it."
The ignorant say that the play of the Lord consists of the moving and unmoving world; yet He is the master over its restraint and its gathering.

That which has fallen on the road remains there protected by destiny, while that which stays at home perishes if struck by Him. Even one who is helpless lives if looked upon by Him in the forest, whereas one protected at home does not live if slain by Him.
Living beings come into existence through their respective actions born of their own origins, and they cease to exist entirely in due time.

In that regard, the Self (ātman) is not bound even when situated within material nature (prakṛti); for it is only one who is identified with the qualities of that nature who is bound by them. This body of the person, born of delusion, is perceived as distinct from the person, just as a house is distinct from its owner.
Just as a person born of water, earth, or fire is transformed and perishes with time;
just as fire is perceived as distinct within pieces of wood; just as the wind, though present within the body, remains separate from it;
and just as the all-pervading sky is not attached to anything—so too is the Supreme Person, the support of all qualities.
"O fools, why do you grieve for this Suyajña who lies here?
He who was the listener and the reciter here can never be seen again.
This chief vital breath (*mahān asu*) is neither the listener nor the reciter in this world."

The self that possesses the senses here is indeed distinct from both the vital breath and the body; for the all-pervading Lord, being other than them, assumes and discards various bodies characterized by elements, senses, and mind,
through His own power.
As long as the self is endowed with the subtle body (liṅga), so long is there bondage to karma;
from that arises the opposite state, suffering, and the persistence of the connection with Māyā.
This false attachment consists of regarding the qualities of nature as objects of value and speaking of them as such.
Just as a desire or a dream, everything pertaining to the senses is false;
therefore, those who know this do not grieve here, whether for what is eternal or impermanent.
It is not possible to act otherwise, for such is the nature of those who grieve.
In the forest, there was a certain hunter appointed as the destroyer of birds;
spreading his net here and there, he lured them in.
There, a pair of *kuliṅga* birds was seen wandering about.
While the two were together, the female sparrow was suddenly enticed by a hunter; she became entangled in the threads of a silken garment, like a queen restrained by her girdle.
Seeing her fallen into such a state, the male sparrow was deeply distressed.
Out of affection, the helpless and wretched man lamented for his miserable wife:
"Alas! The all-powerful Lord is merciless toward this pitiable woman;
what will He do with me, who am so wretched and full of grief as she mourns?"
"Let the Lord take me as He wishes; for what use have I for half of myself, this wretched life of mine, which is full of suffering and a miserable existence?
How indeed shall I support those who are motherless and whose wings have not yet grown?"
"Unfortunate as I am, my young ones are waiting for their mother in the nest.
While the little sparrow was thus lamenting nearby, distressed by separation from his beloved and with a throat choked by tears,
that very fowler— concealed and impelled by Time— pierced him with an arrow.
"Thus, failing to perceive the destruction of your own selves and lacking wisdom,
you shall not find this husband of yours even after hundreds of years, though you may lament.
Thus spoke Śrī Hiraṇyakaśipu.
While the boy was speaking thus, all his kinsmen were struck with wonder in their hearts; they realized that everything is impermanent and arises in a manner that is not as it seems.
Having related this account, Yama vanished right there.
Since Suyajña’s kinsmen have indeed performed for him those rites pertaining to the afterlife, do not grieve for him, nor for others, nor even for yourselves.
For who here is the self, and who is another? Who is one's own, and who belongs to another?
"Without the ignorance that consists of attachment to self and others, [liberation occurs] for embodied beings.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard these words of the lord of the Daityas, Diti, along with her daughter-in-law, [was filled with joy].
Having abandoned his grief for his son in an instant, he fixed his mind upon the ultimate reality.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, Hiraṇyakaśipu was unconquerable, undecaying, and immortal.
He desired to make himself the sole sovereign, without rival;
he performed most rigorous penance in a cave on Mount Mandara,
with his arms raised, his gaze fixed upon the sky, and his body supported by his big toes.
He shone with the rays of his matted hair like the sun at the end of an aeon with its beams.
While he was performing that penance, the gods occupied their respective abodes.
From his head arose smoke-enshrouded fire consisting of the power of his asceticism.
Driven in every direction, he traversed the worlds above, below, and across;
the rivers and oceans were agitated, the earth with its continents and mountains shook,
the stars fell along with the planets, and the ten directions blazed.
Scorched by that [heat], the gods abandoned heaven and went to the world of Brahmā. They informed Dhātṛ:
"O God of gods, Lord of the universe, we are unable to remain in heaven because we have been scorched by the ascetic power of the lord of the Daityas."

O Infinite One, if You so deem it right, bring about his pacification; O Overlord, as long as the worlds do not perish, they shall continue to offer tribute to You. For this was indeed the resolve of him who performed difficult austerities.
Listen; though it may already be known to you, let it nevertheless be told:

having created this world of moving and non-moving beings through austerity, yoga, and meditative absorption, the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) occupies his own throne, which is superior to all other abodes.
Therefore, by means of increasing asceticism, yoga, and meditative absorption, and because both time and the self are eternal, I shall accomplish that for myself;
otherwise, by my own power, I shall ordain this world in a manner different from how it was before.

"What is the use of other [deities] who are swept away by time at the end of the kalpa, such as Viṣṇu and the rest? We have heard this, O Lord of the three worlds; you yourself, having undertaken supreme austerity with steadfast resolve, should now ordain what is appropriate for us."
"O Lord of the World, let your seat for the twice-born and the cows be the supreme state of Brahmā,
for our existence, welfare, prosperity, security, and victory.
Thus addressed by the gods, O King, the Blessed One, who is self-born, [replied].
Surrounded by Bhṛgu, Dakṣa, and others, he went to the hermitage of the lord of the Daityas;
there he did not see [the body], which was concealed by anthills, grass,
and reeds, and covered by ants with its fat, skin, flesh, and blood.
Seeing him heating the worlds with his ascetic power like the sun veiled by clouds,
the one whose vehicle is a swan was struck with wonder and spoke to him with a smile.
Śrī Brahmā said:
"Arise, arise! May it be well with you, O Kāśyapa; you have attained perfection through your austerity. I have come as a granter of boons; choose the boon you desire.
"I have beheld this great wonder within the core of your heart."
The life-breaths of one whose body has been bitten by gadflies indeed rest within the bones.
Neither the sages of old did this, nor will others do so;
for who indeed could sustain their life-breaths without water for a hundred celestial years?
"O son of Diti, by this resolve of yours— difficult for even the high-minded to achieve— and by your steadfastness in austerity, I have been conquered. Therefore,
O bull among the Asuras, I grant you all your boons."
"For the sight of you, who are immortal, is not fruitless for me, O mortal.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the god Ādibhava [Brahmā] [beheld] his body being devoured by ants.
He sprinkled [the ground] with the water from his water-pot, which was divine and possessed unfailing power.
From that hollow bamboo-thicket, he emerged endowed with vigor and strength,
a youth possessed of all limbs and a body as firm as a diamond.
Rising up with the luster of molten gold like a sacrificial fire,
he beheld the Lord stationed in the sky upon his swan-vehicle;
celebrating the great festival of that vision, he bowed his head to the ground.
Rising up, with palms joined in reverence and bowing low, he gazed upon the All-pervading Lord with his eyes;
with tears of joy and the bristling of his hair, he spoke with a voice faltering with emotion.
Śrī Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
At the end of the kalpa, He who is self-luminous, by His own radiance, illumines this world enveloped by the blinding darkness created by Time;
and by means of His threefold nature, He creates, maintains, and withdraws this universe.
Obeisance to the Supreme, the Great One, the abode of passion, goodness, and ignorance; obeisance to the primordial seed, whose form is knowledge and realization,
who attains manifestation through the transformations of the vital breath, senses, mind, and intellect.
You rule over all that moves and all that is stationary as the Lord of creatures by means of the primary vital breath;
you are the Great One, the Lord of the mind through its thoughts, the Lord of the senses, and the Sovereign of the elements, the qualities, and the heart.
You extend the seven threads of sacrifice through your body, by means of the three Vedas and the science of the four officiating priests.
You alone are the beginningless, endless, and boundless Self of those who possess self-mastery, the omniscient inner witness.

You alone are Time, the unblinking one, who wears away the lifespan of living beings through its divisions such as moments and instants. You are the immutable Self, the supreme lord, the unborn, the great; you are the life-force and the very soul of the world of living beings.
There is nothing other than You—neither superior nor inferior, neither unmoving nor moving—that exists apart from You.

All branches of knowledge and all arts are Your bodies; You are Hiraṇyagarbha, the Great One with three backs. O All-pervading Lord, this manifest, gross body is that by which You [perceive] the senses, the vital breaths, the mind, and the qualities.

Abiding in the supreme abode of Brahmā, you enjoy [existence] as the unmanifest Self, the ancient Puruṣa. Salutations to that Blessed One, who is endowed with the powers of consciousness and matter, and by whom this entire universe is pervaded through his infinite and unmanifest form.
O best of givers of boons, if you intend to grant me boons,
O Lord, let there be no death for me from any beings created by you,
whether within or without, by day or by night, nor from any other means or weapons.
Neither on earth nor in the sky was there death for him, neither at the hands of men nor even of beasts; neither by the lifeless nor by the living, nor by gods, asuras, or great serpents,
did he face opposition in battle, for he attained sole sovereignty over all embodied beings.
The majesty of all the world-protectors is like that of his own self;
it never fails through the power of his austerity and yoga.
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus requested, Śatadhṛti, pleased by his penance, then granted those most difficult boons to Hiraṇyakaśipu. Śrī Brahmā said:
"O father, these boons which you choose from me are difficult for men to obtain; nevertheless, my dear son, I shall grant them to you, even though they are hard to attain.
Thereupon, the omnipresent Lord, whose grace is never in vain, departed.
Honored by the best of the asuras and praised by the lords of creatures,
the Daitya, having thus obtained his boon and assuming a body made of gold,
conceived hatred toward the Blessed One, remembering the slaughter of his brother.
Having conquered all the directions and the three worlds, that great asura [subjugated] the lords of gods,
asuras, and humans, the Gandharvas, Garuḍas, and Uragas,
as well as the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Vidyādharas, Ṛṣis, the Lords of the Ancestors (Yama), and the Manus.
Having conquered and brought under his control the lords of the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Pretas, and Bhūtas, as well as the lords of all living beings,
the All-Conqueror took away the positions of the world-protectors along with their splendor.
He dwelt in the celestial realm of Tripiṣṭapa, which was graced with the splendor of divine gardens;
he occupied the palace of Mahendra, built by Viśvakarman himself,
a dwelling-place for the beauty of the three worlds, endowed with every prosperity.
Where the stairs were made of coral and the floors of great emeralds; where the walls were of crystal and the rows of pillars were of lapis lazuli;
where there were variegated canopies and seats of ruby.

The beds, resembling the foam of milk and adorned with coverings of pearl necklaces, were there; and the goddesses, their teeth beautiful, moved here and there making sounds with their tinkling anklets as they beheld their own lovely faces upon the jeweled floors.

In that palace of Mahendra, the mighty and high-minded sole sovereign, who had conquered the worlds and whose fierce commands were formidable, took his pleasure; his pair of feet were worshipped by the gods and others who were humbled by his power.
O dear one, the lords of all the celestial realms beheld him intoxicated with wine, his copper-colored eyes rolling from the potent fragrance of the liquor.

They waited upon Him, the abode of austerity, yoga, strength, and splendor, with their hands empty of offerings; for He was seated by His own power upon the throne of Mahendra. Viśvāvasu, Tumburu, and others like us, O Pāṇḍava, as well as Gandharvas, Siddhas, sages, Vidyādharas, and Apsarases, sang and praised Him repeatedly.

He alone, being worshipped with sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees by those following the system of social classes and stages of life, accepted the portions of the oblations through his own splendor;
for him, the earth consisting of seven continents yielded crops without being ploughed.
Likewise, the cows that grant all desires, the sky which is the locus of various wonders,
and the oceans with their heaps of jewels spoke; and their wives, the rivers,
spoke with their waves consisting of salt water, wine, clarified butter, honey, curds, milk, and nectar-water.
The mountains provided him with pleasure-grounds through their valleys, and the trees bore the qualities of all seasons;
he alone sustained the individual attributes of all the world-protectors.
Thus, having conquered the quarters, that sole sovereign enjoyed his beloved sense-objects.
Just as one who has not conquered his senses is never satisfied while eating according to his pleasure, so it was for him— intoxicated by power, arrogant, acting contrary to the scriptures,
and having incurred the curse of a Brahmin— as a vast period of time passed away.
All the worlds, along with their guardians, being terrified by his fierce punishment and finding no refuge elsewhere, went for shelter to the Imperishable One.
Let there be obeisance to that Direction wherein the Self, the Lord Hari, resides.
"Having gone there, they do not return— those who are peaceful, renounced, and stainless.
Thus, with their selves restrained, their intellects composed, and themselves stainless,
those sages, sleepless and subsisting on air alone, waited upon Hṛṣīkeśa.

To them there appeared a formless voice, resonant like the sound of thunderclouds, filling the quarters of the sky and bestowing fearlessness upon the virtuous: "Do not fear, O best of the wise; may all be well with you."

Indeed, the sight of me leads all living beings to the attainment of every highest good. Since the wickedness of this lowest of the Daityas is now known, I shall bring about his destruction; wait, therefore, for the appointed time.

When there is hatred toward the gods, the Vedas, the cows, the learned brahmins, the virtuous, dharma, and me, that person quickly perishes. [But he who gives] his own daughter to a high-souled man who is free from enmity and tranquil—*bhakti* arises for him. || 27-28 ||
"If he should act with hostility toward Prahlāda, I shall destroy even him, though he be strengthened by boons.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus by the Teacher of the World, the denizens of heaven bowed down to him.
Their agitation subsided and they considered the Asura to be slain.
Of that lord of the Daityas, there were four most wonderful sons; among them, Prahlāda was the greatest, for he was a devotee of Mahat through his virtues.
Devoted to the Brahmanas, endowed with virtuous character, true to his word, and having conquered his senses;
he was the most beloved friend to all beings as if they were himself,
bowing like a servant at the feet of the noble and showing affection for the distressed like a father.

Affectionate toward his peers as toward a brother, regarding his elders with the thought that they are the Lord; rich in learning, wealth, beauty, and noble birth, yet free from the arrogance of pride;
his mind undisturbed even in calamities, devoid of longing for what is heard or seen, he perceives all things as unsubstantial.
O King, he whose senses, vital breaths, body, and intellect are ever restrained, whose desires are forever stilled, and who is free from demonic qualities, is truly a non-asura (asuraḥ).
O King, those great qualities which are repeatedly perceived by the wise in him are not now concealed, just as they are never hidden in the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign.
O King, even the gods, though they are his enemies, hold him up as a model when he sits in the assembly of virtuous singers;
how much more so others like you?
His greatness is indicated by his countless virtues.
He whose natural devotion is fixed upon the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva— like a child who has cast aside his toys because his mind is absorbed in Him,
or like one possessed by the planet Kṛṣṇa— does not perceive this world as it truly is.
Whether sitting, wandering, eating, lying down, drinking,
or speaking, he did not attend to these activities while embraced by Govinda; at times, his consciousness clouded by thoughts of Vaikuṇṭha, he would weep.
Sometimes he laughed, thinking of Him; sometimes, filled with joy, he sang aloud; sometimes, longing for Him, he cried out; and sometimes, free from shame, he danced.
At other times, absorbed in meditation upon Him, he imitated His very nature.
Sometimes, with his hair standing on end, he remains silent, blissful from physical touch,

his eyes closed like lotuses in the waters of the joy of motionless love; this is through his service to the lotus feet of the Lord of Excellent Renown, attained by being free from all worldly attachments.
While repeatedly bestowing upon himself the supreme bliss that pacifies the mind of one wretched by evil association,
O King, Hiraṇyakaśipu committed a sin against that son of his, who was a most fortunate, highly blessed, and great soul.
Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O divine sage of noble vows, we wish to know this from you:
how it was that a father bestowed such an evil upon his own pure and virtuous son.

Fathers who are affectionate toward their children rebuke even their own sons when they act contrary to them, for the sake of instruction and not out of malice; how much more so those who are obedient, virtuous, and like unto gurus and deities?
"O Brahman, O Lord, dispel this curiosity of ours:
how is it that a father's hatred was employed against his own son for the sake of his death?
Śrī Nārada said:
It is said that the venerable Śukra was chosen by the Asuras for the office of family priest;
his two sons, Ṣaṇḍa and Marka, were in the vicinity of the palace of the Daitya king.
There, the king brought the young Prahlāda, who was skilled in policy, before them.
They taught the lessons that were to be learned, as well as other Asura boys;
whatever was spoken there by the teacher, he heard and repeated it back, yet he did not consider it good in his mind, for he was possessed by a perverse attachment to himself and others.
O Pāṇḍava, once the king of the asuras placed his son on his lap and asked, "Tell me, my child, what do you consider to be the highest good? Śrī Prahlāda replied:

O best of asuras, I consider this to be the proper course for embodied beings whose minds are perpetually agitated by attachment to the unreal: having abandoned the home—a pit of darkness that leads to one's own downfall—one should go to the forest and take refuge in Hari.
Śrī Nārada said:
Hearing his sons' words, which were aligned with the opposing side, the Daitya laughed, thinking,
"The intellect of children is swayed by the intellects of others.
"Let this boy be properly maintained in the house of his preceptor by the twice-born."
So that his intellect might not be divided by those disguised as Viṣṇu’s followers,
the priests of the Daityas summoned Prahlāda once he had been brought to their house;
having praised him with gentle words, they questioned him with conciliatory tones.
"My child Prahlāda, may it be well with you; tell me the truth, not a falsehood.
How could this perversion of intellect come to you, who are superior even to children? Was this confusion of mind caused by another, or did it arise from yourself?"
"O delighter of your lineage, please speak to these elders who are eager to hear.
Śrī Prahlāda said:
"The false grasping at 'self' and 'other' among men is created by His illusory power (māyā)."
Salutations to that Blessed One, who is perceived by those whose intellects are deluded.
When a man’s animal-like intelligence, which has fallen into the false state of dualistic distinction—
thinking "this one is other" and "I am other"— is shattered, he becomes devoted to Him.
This very Self, whose sequence of movements is difficult to comprehend for those lacking the discrimination between self and other, is described thus:
even the proponents of the Vedas, beginning with Brahmā, are bewildered regarding His path; indeed, He shatters my mind, O Brahman, just as an iron wheel whirls when brought near a magnet.
"Even so, my heart is pierced by the mere whim of the wielder of the discus.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus to the brāhmaṇa, the high-minded one became silent.
Having rebuked him, the king’s servant became enraged and deeply dejected:
"Let the staff be brought for this one who brings disgrace upon us;
this is the fourth punishment ordained for this evil-minded cinder of his lineage."

"This thorny tree has grown in the sandalwood forest of the Daityas; this child has become the handle for the axe that shall uproot him. Thus he terrified him with various means, such as threats and the like.
He caused Prahlāda to grasp the means for attaining the three goals of life (*trivarga*).
Then, the teacher, knowing that the fourfold objects of knowledge had been understood by him,
presented the Lord of the Daityas— who had been cleansed and adorned by his mother.
The demon, having greeted the boy who had fallen at his feet with a blessing,
embraced him for a long time with both arms and attained supreme bliss;
then, lifting him onto his lap and smelling his head, he [drenched him] with the water-drops of his tears.
As he poured [the water], Yudhiṣṭhira, with his mouth wide open, spoke this;
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O dear Prahlāda, let something well-studied and most excellent be recited."
"O venerable one, in this much time you have learned from your guru.
Śrī Prahlāda said:
"Hearing of Viṣṇu, chanting His names, remembering Him, and serving His feet..."
Worship, salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender—
when devotion characterized by these nine marks is truly offered to Viṣṇu by a person,
I consider that to be the highest study.
Having heard these words of his son, Hiraṇyakaśipu,
his lips quivering with rage, then spoke thus to the preceptor’s son:
"O wretched Brahmin, you who have taken refuge with the enemy, what is this that you say?"
"O evil-minded one, disregarding me, you have led this child to grasp at what is essence-less.
For there are indeed wicked people in the world who wear the mask of friendship while harboring ill intent;
in time, sin arises from them, just as disease arises for the sinful."
The son of the venerable guru said:
"O enemy of Indra, this son of yours speaks neither what is prompted by me nor what is prompted by another.
O King, his intellect is innate; restrain your anger, do not cause us distress."
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus addressed by his preceptor, the Asura spoke again to his son:
"If this is not from the mouth of your guru, whence comes this inauspicious and unchaste thought of yours?"
Śrī Prahlāda said:
The minds of those devoted to the vows of household life do not turn toward Kṛṣṇa, whether through the influence of others, by their own accord, or even among themselves;
they enter the darkness [of ignorance] with their senses unsubdued, repeatedly chewing over what has already been chewed.

Those of wicked intent, who consider external objects to be the highest goal, do not know Viṣṇu, the path to their own true welfare. Like blind men led by the blind, they too are bound by the vast fetters of the Lord’s sovereignty. Their intellect does not touch the feet of the Wide-Striding One until there is the removal of that misfortune for which [the realization of Him] is the purpose.

"Until one has received the sprinkling of the dust from the feet of the Great Ones, one should not choose [anything else] for oneself, being free from possessions. Having spoken thus, Hiraṇyakaśipu, his mind blinded by rage, cast his son down from his lap onto the surface of the earth.
Overcome with indignation and rage, his eyes turning blood-red, he said:
"Let this man be killed immediately; he deserves to be slain! Drive him away, O Rākṣasas!
This is the killer of my brother; this lowest of men has abandoned his own kinsmen and friends."
He who worships the feet of Viṣṇu like a servant— even if he is the killer of his paternal uncle—
what can that unrighteous man do to Viṣṇu? For even a five-year-old child cannot abandon affection for its parents.
Even a stranger is like beneficial medicine if he acts for one's welfare, whereas a son born of one's own body is like a disease if he is harmful.
One should cut off that limb which is detrimental to oneself, for by its removal, the remainder lives happily.
A son who is harmful must be destroyed by all possible means—by depriving him of food, sleep, and even his seat.
Bearing the outward marks of a friend, he was an enemy like a wicked sense-organ of a sage.
Those Nairṛtas were commanded by their lord; they carried tridents in their hands, with mouths made terrifying by sharp fangs, and possessed copper-colored beards and hair.
Uttering a terrifying roar and crying out, "Cut him! Pierce him!",
they struck Prahlāda— who was seated within the Lord, the indefinable Supreme Brahman and the Self of all— with spears in every vital organ.

When his efforts were frustrated, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the lord of the Daityas became apprehensive and, with persistence, devised means for his destruction— just as virtuous deeds bear no fruit for one whose merit has not yet ripened, even though he is self-disciplined.
By means of world-elephants, lordly serpents, malevolent incantations, and the causing of falls; by illusions, imprisonments, the administration of poison, and starvation;
and even by cold, wind, fire, water, and the crushing of mountains.
When the asura was unable to kill his sinless son,
he fell into deep anxiety and could not find a way to achieve it.
"I have spoken many unwholesome words and devised various means for his destruction."
Though he was released from those various acts of hostility and unrighteousness by his own splendor,
this boy— even though he is but a child— possesses an undull intellect; remaining close at hand,
this lord does not forget my ignoble conduct, just as Śunaḥśepa did not.
"This one of immeasurable power is fearless and immortal;
surely my death will come through conflict with him, or perhaps not.
Thinking thus, her splendor somewhat faded, she stood with her face cast downward.
Śaṇḍa and Marka, the two sons of Śukrācārya, said in private:

"O Lord, by you alone, with the mere knitting of your eyebrows, the entire three worlds have been conquered, causing all the presiding deities to tremble. We do not consider that to be something to be worried about; indeed, children are beyond the reach of both virtue and vice."
"Bind him with the nooses of Varuṇa so that, being terrified, he does not flee. And let his intellect be clouded by old age until the preceptor Bhārgava returns.
Having assented to these words of the preceptor's son, saying "So be it," he spoke as follows:
O King, he indeed taught the dharma for householders to Prahlāda,
who was humble and bowed before him— the dharma, wealth, and pleasure, each in its proper order and with great thoroughness.
Just as he did not consider the three-fold aims (trivarga) taught by his teachers for himself to be beneficial— since that instruction was described as delighting in the pairs of opposites—
so too when the teacher turned away from the duties of a householder.
There, he was invited by his companions, the boys who were waiting for him;
then the great sage, the wise one, having called them back with gentle words, spoke out of compassion as if smiling, regarding their devotion to that [game].

Out of respect for him, O King of kings, all those children— having abandoned their playthings and their uncorrupted minds being moved by the activities of the pairs of opposites— waited upon him with their hearts and eyes fixed upon him.
The compassionate and friendly Asura, a great devotee of the Lord, spoke to them;
Śrī Prahlāda said:
"In this world, a wise person in his youth should practice the Bhāgavata duties."
Human birth is difficult to attain, and even that is impermanent and yields worldly results; yet it is possible for a person here to approach the feet of Viṣṇu,
for He is the beloved Self, the Lord, and the Friend of all living beings.
O Daityas, sense-based happiness for embodied beings is obtained everywhere through the connection with a body by the force of destiny, just as suffering is obtained effortlessly; therefore,
one should not exert effort for it, since it results only in the waste of life.
One does not find such security elsewhere as in the lotus feet of Mukunda; therefore,
a person of skill who has entered this cycle of existence should strive for that security while the human body remains fully intact and before it perishes.

The lifespan of a human being is indeed one hundred years; half of that is fruitless for one who has not conquered the self, as he sleeps at night, having been led into blinding darkness. Twenty years pass while he is infatuated, playing in childhood and youth.

For one whose body is seized by old age and who is incapable, twenty years pass away; for one who is attached to his home and intoxicated, the remainder of life indeed slips away through insatiable desire and powerful delusion.

What man, lacking self-control, would be able to liberate himself when he is bound by the firm snares of affection within his home? And who indeed would cast away the thirst for wealth, which is desired even more than life itself?
How can a thief, a servant, or a merchant— who purchases with his most beloved vital breaths—

the secret association, the private conversations, and the charming words of his beloved and compassionate wife; how can one whose heart is devoted to the lisping syllables of children, who is bound by affection for them, share such things with friends?
Remembering his sons, those beloved daughters, brothers, sisters, and his distressed parents;

his charming home with its abundant furnishings, his ancestral livelihoods, and his flocks of cattle and servants— who, like a caterpillar moving from leaf to leaf, would abandon these while still yearning for them out of greed, his desires remaining unsatiated?
How could one whose delusion is insurmountable become detached while highly esteeming the pleasures of the genitals and the tongue?
Being intoxicated, he does not perceive that his own life is wasting away for the sake of nourishing his family, nor does he realize his lost purpose.
With his soul suffering from the threefold miseries everywhere, he finds no revulsion even though he is attached to his own family.
O sons of Danu, even a learned man whose mind is constantly attached to wealth, though he knows the fault of one who steals another's property—

whether in this world or after death— and yet, with uncontrolled senses and unappeased desires, continues to take it for the sake of his family; even such a learned man, O Danujas, while nourishing his family in this manner, is certainly not fit for his own higher worlds.
He who, being deluded, would fall into the darkness of the notion that his own self and the Supreme are distinct—

since no one, anywhere, at any time, or in any way, is sufficiently capable of liberating his own wretched self from the fetters of material existence, which is but a plaything for those who gaze upon their desires.

Then, having avoided from afar the company of the Daityas who are devoted to sense objects, he approached Nārāyaṇa, the primordial God; for he was impelled by those free from attachment toward liberation.
O sons of the Asuras, there is indeed no great exertion for one who pleases Acyuta.
Because he is the self of all beings, he is established everywhere here— in all beings,
high and low, from Brahmā down to the stationary objects; in material transformations, in the elements, and likewise in the great elements.
In the modes of nature, in their state of equilibrium, and likewise in their mutual transformation,
there is indeed only one Supreme Self— the immutable Lord and Master—
who exists as both the nature of the individual soul (*pratyagātman*) and the form of the perceptible world itself.

The Supreme Lord, whose essential nature is absolute experiential bliss, is indeed both definable as the pervaded and the pervader, yet ultimately indefinable and free from conceptual construction; though His sovereignty is concealed by *māyā*, He is perceived through the manifestation of the qualities (*guṇa-sarga*).
Therefore, abandon the demoniac disposition and practice compassion and friendship toward all beings,
by which Adhokṣaja is pleased. When He— the infinite and primordial— is satisfied, what is there that cannot be obtained?

What need have we here for those qualities such as dharma, which are established by their own nature through the intermixture of the *guṇas*, or for that which is desired from the *aguṇa* (the unconditioned)? For us, let there be only the chanting of the essence of the feet of those who delight in the Supreme.

That which is called the threefold aggregate of dharma, artha, and kāma; the science of inquiry, the three Vedas, statesmanship, and the various forms of economic activity— I consider all this to be the truth of the Veda.
The surrender of one’s own self to the Supreme Person, who is one’s own true friend—
this very knowledge, which is stainless and difficult to attain,
was indeed spoken by Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara, to Nārada.
For those who are single-mindedly devoted to the Blessed One, who possess nothing,
and whose bodies are bathed in the dust of his lotus feet—
this knowledge, conjoined with realized wisdom, was previously heard by me.
From Nārada, who has the vision of the Divine, they received the pure, Bhāgavata dharma.
The sons of the Daitya said:
"O Prahlāda, both you and we know no teacher other than him."
"These two sons of the guru are indeed masters even over children.
For a child staying within the inner apartments, association with the great is difficult to sever.
O gentle one, please cut through our doubt if there is a cause for confidence."
Śrī Nārada said: Thus questioned by the sons of the Daityas, the great devotee of the Lord, that Asura,
smiling and recollecting my words, spoke to them.
Śrī Prahlāda said:
When our father had departed for Mount Mandara to perform austerities,
the gods made a supreme effort to wage war against the Dānavas.

"By good fortune, this sinful oppressor of the world has been devoured by a wicked serpent, like a termite!"— thus spoke Vāsava and the other gods. Hearing of their exceedingly powerful exertion, the leaders of the demon hosts [prepared for battle].

Being struck by the gods and filled with fear, they fled in every direction; not looking back at their wives, sons, wealth, kinsmen, homes, cattle, or belongings, they all hurried away, desiring only to save their lives.
Desiring victory, the immortals plundered the royal camp;
Indra, however, seized the queen, my mother,
as she was being led away, agitated by fear and weeping like a female osprey.
By chance, the celestial sage Nārada arrived there on the path and saw her;
he said, "O Lord of the Gods, you ought not to carry off this innocent woman.
Release her, release her, O illustrious one! She is a virtuous wife belonging to another."
Śrī Indra said:
"The unbearable seed of the enemy of the gods lies within her womb. Remain here until her delivery; once she has given birth, I shall attain my goal."
Śrī Nārada said:
This great and mighty devotee of the Lord, who is free from all sin and an attendant of Ananta, will not meet his end at your hands.
Thus addressed, Indra, honoring the words of the celestial sage, abandoned her;
out of devotion to the Beloved of Ananta, he circumambulated her and departed for heaven.
Then the sage, having brought my mother to his own hermitage, [proceeded].
"Be comforted, my child; you shall dwell here until your husband returns.
Saying "So be it," she lived near the celestial sage, free from fear from any quarter, until the lord of the Daityas ceased his terrible ascetic penance.
There, the virtuous woman served the sage with supreme devotion,
being pregnant and desiring the welfare of her embryo and its timely birth.
The compassionate sage, who was her lord, granted her both these things.

The stainless truth of dharma and knowledge concerning me were revealed; however, due to the length of time and my female nature, they vanished from my mother. Yet, because I was favored by the sage, that memory has not left me even until now.

If you have faith in my words, then even for you there shall arise a profound and confident wisdom, just as it has arisen in women and children through faith. These six states— birth and the rest— are observed to belong to the body, not to the self.
Just as the fruits of a tree [are shed] by Time in the form of the Lord, so too the Self— the eternal, immutable, pure, singular Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the substratum,
changeless, self-perceiving cause, all-pervading, unattached, and unobscured— is [separated].
By means of these twelve supreme characteristics of the self,
the wise man should abandon the unreal notion of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, which arises from delusion.
Just as a goldsmith skilled in its nature obtains gold from among stones by various methods, so too does he obtain it from among the fields [of the senses].

Likewise, through self-yoga within the fields of the bodies, one who knows the supreme self attains the state of Brahman. Eight are declared to be the primary natures (*prakṛti*), and indeed only three are their qualities (*guṇa*).
The teachers say there are sixteen transformations (*vikāra*), and the person (*puruṣa*) is one because of his pervasive connection with them.
The body, however, is a composite of all [elements], divided into two types: the moving (jagat) and the stationary (tasthuḥ).

Within this very [body] is the Person (puruṣa) to be sought by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) and through discrimination (viveka), while abandoning that which is not the Self (neti neti).
By those who have attained the abodes of heaven and who reflect with composure through the traditional scriptures,
it is understood that waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are the functions of the intellect;
he by whom these are experienced is the Supreme Person, the Witness.
Through these three castes, which are encompassed by various distinctions of intellect arising from ritual actions,
one should perceive the true nature of the self, just as one perceives the wind through its associated fragrances.
For this world-process, bound by the qualities (*guṇas*) and their corresponding actions, has these [distinctions] as its gateway.
Rooted in ignorance, this meaningless state is presented to man like a dream.
Therefore, you must perform that yoga which uproots the seeds of actions born of the three modes of nature and brings the flow of the intellect to rest.
Among thousands of means for that end, this one has been declared by the Blessed Lord:
that by which and in what manner one may easily attain devotion toward the Sovereign,
the Blessed One— through service to the guru, through devotion, and by offering all that has been acquired.
Through association with the devotees of the virtuous, through the worship of the Lord, through faith in His stories, through the chanting of His qualities and deeds,
through meditation upon His lotus feet, and through beholding and honoring His symbols;
"The Lord Hari, the Sovereign, dwells within all beings"—
thinking thus, one should properly honor all beings with one's mind and according to their desires.
In this way, by those who have conquered the six internal enemies, devotion to the Lord is cultivated.

When, upon hearing of the incomparable deeds, qualities, and heroic exploits performed by the Lord Vāsudeva through his incarnate forms, one attains a state of intense delight characterized by horripilation, tears, and a faltering voice, and one sings aloud, cries out, or dances with yearning; [then that is the attainment of love for the Blessed One.]
When, as if seized by a planet, he sometimes laughs, cries out, meditates, or bows down to people;

when, sighing repeatedly, he speaks the words "O Hari, Lord of the World! O Nārāyaṇa!"—his mind fixed on Him and free from shame—then that man is liberated from all bonds, his heart and appearance having been transformed by the influence of His own state of being.
Having completely burnt away the latent tendencies of the seeds [of karma] through the practice of supreme devotion, one meets Adhokṣaja.

O Brahmin, the wise know that attaining Adhokṣaja here for an embodied soul whose nature was impure destroys the wheel of worldly existence; it is the bliss of liberation in Brahman. Therefore, worship the Lord of the Heart within your own hearts.

O children of the asuras, what great effort is required to worship Hari, who dwells within one's own heart like a hole? He is one's own Self, the friend of all embodied beings; what need is there for the procurement of sense objects?
Wealth, wife, cattle, sons and others, houses, land, elephants, treasuries, and prosperity— *BhP 07.07.038–039*
All objects of desire, which are as fleeting as a momentary lifespan, can provide only a small measure of pleasure to a mortal; for they are unstable.
Indeed, these worlds created by sacrifices are perishable, subject to comparison, and not pure.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining the Self, one should worship with devotion the Supreme Lord, whose faults have never been seen or heard of.
O learned one, for whatever purpose a man of honor repeatedly performs actions in this world, he obtains from them a fruit that is never in vain;
yet the resolve of the ritualist here is directed toward pleasure and the escape from suffering.

One who is free from worldly striving is ever enveloped in happiness, whereas one who strives here always obtains suffering. That body for the sake of which a person desires objects of desire through various means of enjoyment is indeed alien, fragile, and subject to coming and going.
How much less so, then, are distant offspring, wives, houses, wealth, and the like—
kingdoms, treasuries, elephants, ministers, servants, and kinsmen, which are merely objects of one's sense of "mine-ness"?
What is the use of these trivial things for the self, along with this perishable body?

O demons, how much of one's own true interest can be discerned here in this world by embodied beings who are tormented by their karmas throughout stages beginning with conception, when that interest is pursued through objects which appear to be goals but are actually worthless, compared to the ocean of the essence of eternal bliss?
The embodied soul undertakes actions with a body that follows the self; through those actions, it expands the body. Both of these, however, arise from a lack of discrimination.
Therefore, material objects, desires, and religious duties all depend upon this [discrimination].
One should worship with desireless devotion Hari, the Lord, who is Himself free from desire. For all beings, Hari is the Self, the Lord, and the Beloved;
He is known as the individual soul (jīva) within those created by the great elements fashioned by His own power.
Whether a god, an asura, a human, a yakṣa, or even a gandharva,
by worshipping the feet of Mukunda one shall attain well-being, just as we have.
O sons of the asuras, neither the status of the twice-born, nor divinity, nor the state of a ṛṣi is sufficient [for this].
Neither conduct, nor great learning, nor charity, nor austerity, nor sacrifice, nor purity, nor vows please Mukunda;
Hari is pleased by stainless devotion alone— everything else is mere mockery.
"Therefore, O Dānavas, cultivate devotion toward Hari, the Blessed Lord,
by regarding all beings with the same equanimity as yourselves, for He is the Lord and the Self of all beings.
Whether they be Daityas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, women, Śūdras, or residents of Vraja,"
Even birds, wild animals, and those who live by sinful means have indeed attained the state of Acyuta.
This alone is considered the supreme self-interest for a person in this world:
exclusive devotion to Govinda and perceiving Him everywhere.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then all the sons of the Daityas, having heard that description,
did not at all accept the instruction given by their preceptor because of its faultlessness.

Then the preceptor’s son, perceiving that their minds were fixed one-pointedly on Him, became alarmed and quickly reported it to the king exactly as it was. Upon hearing of that unpleasant and unbearable misconduct of his sons, the Daitya [was filled with distress].

With his limbs trembling from the onset of anger, he set his mind on killing his son; having reviled Prahlāda— who was undeserving of such treatment— with harsh words, he spoke while looking at him with an evil, sidelong glance.
To him who stood bowed in humility, self-controlled, with palms joined in reverence,
the serpent Hiraṇyakaśipu— naturally cruel and hissing like one trodden upon by a foot—
spoke.

"O ill-behaved one, O dull-witted one, O lowest of those who cause the destruction of their lineage! You are arrogant and have transgressed my command; today I shall send you to the abode of Yama—[the god] at whose wrath the three worlds, together with their lords, tremble."
"O fool, why have you disregarded my command as if you were fearless? Why, O Bāṇa, did you transgress it? Śrī Prahlāda said:
"O King, that strength belongs not only to me, nor even to you, but indeed to all other powerful beings as well."
He by whom all these—those higher and lower, the moving and the stationary, beginning with Brahmā—have been brought under control;
He is the Lord, Time, the Wide-striding One (Urukrama), the essence of vigor, endurance, strength, the modes of nature, the senses, and the self.
He alone, the Supreme Lord of the three qualities, creates, maintains, and devours the universe by means of His own powers.

Abandon this demonic disposition of yours and make your mind equanimous; there are no enemies other than the unconquered self that has strayed onto the wrong path, for its conquest is indeed the great worship of the Infinite One.
Some consider the ten directions already conquered when one merely defeats the plundering bandits.
For one who has conquered the self, who is wise, equanimous toward all embodied beings, and virtuous—whence could there be others born of his own delusion?
Śrī Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
It is evident that you desire to die, since you boast so excessively.
O dull-witted one, indeed the words of those about to die are surely faltering.
As for that other Lord of the Universe whom you, unfortunate as you are, have spoken of—where is He? If He is everywhere, why is He not seen in this pillar?
"I shall sever from your body the head of you who boast so much! May Hari protect you today, he whom you seek as your refuge.
Thus, with harsh words, the great demon repeatedly tormented his son, the illustrious devotee of the Lord, out of rage.
Seizing his sword, the exceedingly powerful one sprang from his excellent seat and struck the pillar with his own fist.
At that very moment, an extremely terrifying roar arose within it, by which the shell of the cosmic egg was shattered;
hearing this, O dear one, Brahmā and the other gods, who had returned to their own abodes, thought their own worlds were coming to an end.
Striding with vigor and desiring the slaughter of his sons, he heard an unprecedented and wonderful roar;
yet, within the assembly hall, he could not perceive its source, by which the leaders of the hosts of the enemies of the gods were struck with terror.
This was so that He might make true the words spoken by His own servant and manifest His pervasion throughout all beings.
Bearing a most wonderful form that was invisible [to others], neither beast nor human, he stood in the assembly hall within the pillar.
Surveying this being all around him as it emerged from the middle of the pillar, he thought:
"This is neither a beast nor a man; oh, what a marvel! What is this extraordinary form of a lion among men?"
As he was thus reflecting, there arose before him the form of Nṛsiṃha, which was utterly terrifying,
with fierce eyes like molten gold, a face expanded by a mane of quivering hair,
formidable tusks, a tongue flickering like a sword with razor-sharp edges, and a countenance made fierce by a frown upon his brow.
With stiff, upright ears, a gaping mouth and nose as vast as a mountain cave, and terrifying with its split jaw;
with a body touching the heavens, a long and thick neck, broad chest, and narrow waist;
covered all over with body hair white as the rays of the moon, he possessed hundreds of arms as his army, with nails for weapons.

"Difficult to approach, with all other weapons rendered useless and the Daityas and Dānavas put to flight by the excellence of [his] weaponry— will this death of mine likely come at the hands of this Hari, who is now prepared with his great illusory power?
Speaking thus, that elephant among Daityas, roaring and armed with a mace, rushed toward Narasiṃha.

Unobserved, that asura fell into the fire of Nṛsiṃha’s splendor like a moth; yet this was not surprising for him who, in the past, had swallowed the darkness by his own power within the abode of pure being.
Then, rushing forward in rage, the great asura struck Nṛsiṃha with a mace of immense velocity.
As he was charging with his mace, Gadādhara seized him just as the son of Tārkṣya seizes a great serpent;
then that demon, released from his hand, was like a snake dropped by Garuḍa while he was sporting.
O descendant of Bharata, the immortals who dwell in all the celestial abodes, their own domains having been taken away, considered this to be improper, for they were shrouded by thick clouds.
Thinking that Nṛhari was intimidated by his own prowess, the great asura,
grasping sword and shield, again attacked him with speed in the battle, his fatigue gone;
while Hari moved above and below without interruption, following the path of the hawk’s swoop marked by a hundred moons.
Letting out a loud, harsh, and resonant roar, Hari, possessing great speed, seized him with eyes closed;
as he quivered in every direction, distressed by the capture, Hari— whose skin was unscarred by the thunderbolt—
seized him at the thigh by the door and effortlessly tore him apart with his claws, just as Garuḍa tears apart a highly venomous serpent.
With eyes fierce and terrible to behold due to his fury, licking the corners of his gaping mouth with his tongue,
his face and mane reddened by drops of blood— like a lion after slaying an elephant, garlanded with entrails—
he cast aside the lotus-heart torn out by the tip of his claw, leaving behind the demon’s followers who stood with weapons raised.
With his thousands of staff-like arms, he slew with his nails as weapons all those who followed him by the thousands.
Clouds were blown away by the shaking of his mane, and the planets fell, their luster stolen by his gaze.
The oceans, struck by his breath, were agitated; the elephants of the quarters cried out, terrified by his roar.
The sky became crowded with celestial chariots tossed upward by his hair, and the earth, pressed down by his feet, sank away.
The mountains leaped up at his speed, and by his splendor, neither the firmament nor the quarters of the sky shone.
Then, the Lord, whose splendor was fully gathered, sat upon an excellent royal throne in the assembly hall.

No one could face that first-born Daitya, whose fierce countenance was unyielding and whose fury in the duel was unnoticed; yet, upon seeing him— the fever of the heads of the three worlds— slain by Hari in battle,
the celestial women, their faces upturned with a surge of joy, repeatedly rained down showers of flowers.

Then the vault of the sky became crowded with rows of celestial chariots belonging to the gods who desired to behold [the Lord]; divine kettledrums and dundubhi drums were struck, the chief Gandharvas danced, and the women sang. Having approached there, the gods led by Brahmā, Indra, and Giriśa—
The sages, the ancestors, the perfected ones, the Vidyādharas, the great serpents, the Manus, the lords of creatures, the Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Cāraṇas;
the Yakṣas, Kimpuruṣas, Vetālas, and Kinnaras, O dear one— *Note: This translation reflects the continuity of the verses as they appear in the source text.*
All those attendants of Viṣṇu, headed by Sunanda and Kumuda,
standing not too far away with their palms joined in reverence upon their heads, individually praised that tiger among men as he sat there, blazing with intense splendor.
Śrī Brahmā said:
I bow down to the Infinite One, whose power is boundless, who possesses diverse prowess, and whose actions are purifying;
to the Imperishable Self who, by means of His own qualities, effects through His divine play the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.
Śrī Rudra said:
"The time for your anger is the end of the age; that insignificant demon has been slain.
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, protect his son who has approached you as a devotee."
Śrī Indra said:
O Supreme One, our own shares have been restored by You, our protector;
the lotus-heart that had been seized by the Daityas has been awakened as Your dwelling place.
"O Lord, how insignificant is this world seized by Time for those who desire to serve You!
Is liberation not highly esteemed by them, any more than it is by the followers of Nṛsiṃha?
The Śrī-Ṛṣis said:

O Protector of those who seek refuge, You have told us that supreme austerity is Your own spiritual splendor, by which You, as the Original Person, created this universe residing within Yourself; yet that has been stolen away by this one today.
Furthermore, assuming the form of a Rakshasa, You have granted Your permission [for our sacrifice].
The venerable fathers said:
"Our *śrāddha* offerings were forcibly consumed by Your sons."
He drank the water mixed with sesame seeds that had been offered at the time of a sacred pilgrimage;
his body was torn open by His claws, and from his belly He rescued [the devotee].
Homage to Him, Nṛhari, the protector of all dharma!

The Śrīsiddhas said: O Nṛsiṃha, we bow down to You, who with the claws of Your nails tore apart that wicked one who, by the power of his yoga and austerity, stole from us our goal— the perfection of yoga— and our various forms of pride.
The Vidyādharas said:

We perpetually bow down to that Māyā-Nṛsiṃha, by whom he— who was ignorant, arrogant in his strength and heroism, and who had prohibited the various sciences mastered through yogic concentration— was slain in battle like a mere beast.
The Śrī-nāgas said:
"O Giver of Bliss, salutations be to You, by whose chest being torn open, the sin by which our jewels and the jewel among women was stolen shall be destroyed."
The Śrīmanus said:
"O Lord, we are the Manus, the executors of your commands; our moral boundaries have been violated by the son of Diti.
O Master, that wicked one has been destroyed by you. What shall we do for you? Command us, your servants."
The Prajāpatis said: "O Supreme Lord, we are the lords of progeny created by You; yet, forbidden by You, we were unable to create offspring.
That very incarnation of Yours, the embodiment of goodness and the auspiciousness of the world, now lies here with his chest pierced."
The illustrious Gandharvas said:
"O All-pervading Lord, we are Your dancers, actors, and singers, who have been brought under Your own control by Your prowess, strength, and splendor.
Yet You have reduced him to this state; for how can one who stands on a wrong path lead to well-being?"
The celestial singers said:
O Hari, we have taken refuge at Your lotus feet, which grant liberation from worldly existence,
since this demon who dwelt in the hearts of the virtuous has been destroyed by You.
The Śrī-yakṣas said:
"We are the chief attendants [of the Lord] by virtue of our pleasing deeds;
yet here we have been reduced to the state of being his bearers by this son of Diti."
But he, Nṛhari, knowing the suffering caused to the people by him,
brought that twenty-fifth principle to its end;
thus spoke the Śrī-Kimpuruṣas.
"We are mere *kiṃpuruṣas*, whereas you are the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*), the Lord. This wicked man has perished, censured by the virtuous.
Thus spoke the royal bards.

"In the assemblies and sacrificial sessions, by singing Your stainless glory, we receive great honor; yet this wicked man has brought that very honor to its ruin. O Blessed One, may he be struck down by Your hatred, just as a disease is destroyed.
Thus spoke the Śrī-kinnaras.

"O Lord, we are hosts of *kinnaras* who are your followers; yet we have been compelled into this forced labor by this son of Diti. O Hari, O Narasiṃha, O Master, that evildoer has been destroyed by you; please be for our prosperity.
Thus spoke the attendants of Śrī Viṣṇu.
O Giver of Refuge, O Bestower of Happiness to all the worlds, this wonderful form of Yours as a lion-man has today been seen by us.
O Lord, we understand that this man, cursed by the brahmins, was Your servant; we know that his death was for the sake of Your grace.
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus, all the gods and others, led by Brahmā and Rudra,
were unable to approach his most difficult-to-assail fury and agitation;
for Śrī herself had been sent by the gods upon seeing that great wonder.
Because she had never seen or heard of such a thing before, she was filled with doubt and did not approach him;
instead, she sent Prahlāda, who was standing nearby, saying:
"O dear one, go and pacify the Lord, who is angry with your father."
"So be it," O King, the great devotee replied softly; approaching him, the boy bowed down to the ground with his body, holding his hands in reverence.
Seeing that child fallen at the soles of his feet, the Lord was overwhelmed with compassion.
Raising him up, He placed His lotus hand upon his head—a hand that grants fearlessness to those terrified by the serpent of Time.
By the touch of His hand, all his inauspiciousness was shaken off, and the vision of the Supreme Self was immediately revealed to him.
With his body bristling with joy, his heart melting and his eyes filled with tears, he felt profound peace as he held His lotus feet within his own heart.
With his mind one-pointed and perfectly composed,
he praised Hari with a voice faltering with love, his heart and gaze fixed upon Him.
Śrī Prahlāda said:

Even now, the hosts of gods headed by Brahmā, the sages, and the perfected ones (siddhas)— whose minds were entirely absorbed in pure goodness— were not able to satisfy Him with floods of words, however many their virtues.
Why should Hari be pleased with me, born of a fierce lineage?
I consider wealth, noble birth, beauty, austerity, learning,
vigor, splendor, majesty, strength, manliness, and intelligence— these are merely the products of yoga.
For these do not lead to the propitiation of the Supreme Person;
yet the Blessed One was pleased by devotion even in the case of the leader of the elephant herd.
O Lotus-navelled One, [grant me grace] from the Brahmin who is endowed with the six qualities and reverence.

I consider even a dog-eater (outcaste) to be superior to one who turns his back on the lotus feet of the Lord; for he whose mind, speech, actions, wealth, and life-breath are dedicated to Him purifies his entire lineage, whereas one who is full of great pride does not.
This compassionate Lord, who is full of His own attainment, does not seek honor from ignorant people;
yet whatever honor a person may offer to the Blessed One, [He accepts].
And just as the beauty of a face is reflected in a mirror held before it,
so do I, freed from all agitation, praise with my whole being the majesty of the Lord according to my understanding.
By the description of which even a base person who has entered into the discharge of the modes may be purified—
indeed, all these performers of ritual injunctions belong to you, the abode of pure goodness.
O Lord, even we, headed by Brahmā, are not as agitated as these people;
therefore, for their security, prosperity, and for their own happiness,
please manifest the playful pastimes of the Blessed One through beautiful incarnations.
Therefore, restrain your anger; for the asura has been slain by you today.
A virtuous man may even rejoice at the killing of a scorpion or a snake, and all the worlds shall attain peace and turn back from their distress.
O Nṛsiṃha, people remember Your form for the sake of fearlessness;
yet I do not fear You, O Unconquered One, though Your face is most terrifying, with its tongue like the sun, eyes like the sun, frowning brows, and fierce fangs.
I am terrified by those whose garlands are entrails, whose manes are blood, and whose ears are like spikes;

who cause the elephants of the quarters to flee in fear with their roar, and who tear apart enemies with the tips of their claws— O you who are compassionate toward the wretched, I am afraid of this unbearable and fierce [demon].
O Most Exalted One, when will You, being pleased, call me— who am tormented by the wheel of saṃsāra, seized and bound by my own karmas— to the root of Your feet, the refuge of liberation?
Because, born from the separation from the beloved and union with the unpleasant,
I am being burned by the fire of grief in all wombs; therefore,
though it is a medicine for suffering, I perceive even that as suffering due to my lack of realization of the Truth.
O Infinite One, I wander in delusion; tell me the yoga of service unto You.
O Nṛsiṃha, I am that very person who sings the playful stories of You—the beloved friend, the supreme deity—as they were sung by Viriñca.
Chanting [Your names] directly, one who is liberated from the material qualities easily crosses over all difficulties through association with the swans that take refuge at Your pair of feet.
O Nṛsiṃha, for a child in this world, the parents are not a true shelter.

O All-pervading Lord, for embodied beings who are afflicted, there is no remedy as direct as medicine for one in pain, nor a boat for one sinking in the ocean; such is the means of relief for those whom You have neglected in this world.
In whom, from whom, at what time, by what means, for whom, from what cause, for what purpose, in what manner, and whatever state— whether inferior or superior—
it performs or transforms, being of a distinct nature; [all this is the Lord].
Thus impelled, that entire nature of yours—
the mind— creates through the power of karma,
urged by time and sanctioned by the qualities (guṇas) of the person.
