O Unborn One, who other than You could cross over this wheel of worldly existence, which consists of the Vedic meters and has sixteen spokes offered by Ajā? For You, O Lord, have eternally conquered the qualities of the self through Your own splendor.
O Lord, Time, whose power to create and withdraw has brought all things under its control,
has cast me upon this wheel of sixteen spokes;
O All-pervading One, draw back that which is being crushed, for I have sought refuge in You.
O All-pervading Lord, I have seen in heaven the lifespan, prosperity, and power of all the guardians of the celestial realms— those which this world desires—
and those [powers] which were manifested by the knitting of the eyebrows of my father when he was provoked to anger.
But he was repelled by its thunderous roar;
therefore, O ignorant one, I am not the desired objects of embodied beings—
namely life, prosperity, power, and sensory gratification— extending even unto Brahmā.
I do not desire those blessings of yours, O Lord of great prowess, which are agitated by you whose nature is Time; lead me instead to the side of your own servants.
Where are those blessings that are pleasant to the ear, yet are merely like a mirage?

Where is this body, the breeding ground for every kind of disease, that people do not become weary of it even though they know its nature? They seek to extinguish the fire of desire with drops of honey that are difficult to obtain.
O Lord, where am I— born of the mode of passion (*rajas*) in this world of predominant darkness (*tamas*),
born into a family of non-gods— and where is Your compassion? It is not found in Brahmā, nor in Śiva, nor indeed in Lakṣmī.
That Your lotus-hand was placed upon my head as a mark of grace—
surely this is not the mind of one who distinguishes between high and low, for You are the well-wisher of all beings in the world as You are of Yourself.
Your grace is like that of the celestial wish-fulfilling tree;
it arises in accordance with one's service, not according to whether one is superior or inferior. Thus, people have fallen into the well of the serpent of worldly existence.
O Blessed One, how could I ever abandon service to Your servant, I who, falling through attachment into a pursuit of desires, was taken into my own heart by the divine sage?
O Ananta, I consider the protection of my life and the killing of my father to have been for the purpose of making true the words of the sage, my own servant,
which he spoke while grasping his sword, desiring to do what was improper.
May the Lord, who is indifferent to my pride, protect you; whom else shall I take refuge in?
You alone are this entire universe, for you exist separately at its beginning and end, as well as in its middle.
Having created this world through Your own *māyā* by the intermingling of the *guṇas*, You appear as if diverse through them;
yet, having entered into it, You remain within it. O Lord, You are both this existent and non-existent world, and yet You are other than that.
This notion of "self" and "other" is indeed a useless illusion;
for whatever birth, death, maintenance, or perception belongs to one thing, that very same [birth, etc. belongs to the other, just as wealth and time are shared by both a tree and its owner.
Having cast this universe into the waters of dissolution within Himself, He remains by His own nature,
experiencing His own bliss, free from desire,
with eyes closed through yoga and sleep swallowed up within the Self.
Established in the fourth state (turiya), you are joined neither with darkness (tamas) nor with the qualities (guṇas).
This form of yours is hidden by the Self, its material nature (prakṛti) impelled by Your own power of time (kāla-śakti).
From the navel of Ananta-śayana, as he ceased from his samādhi within the waters, there arose a great lotus like a hollowed-out seed-pod; from that lotus was born the Sage (Brahmā),
who perceived nothing other than him.

Having contemplated you as the seed pervading his own self and yet existing outside, he searched for it by immersing himself in water for a hundred years; once the sprout had emerged, how could he possibly perceive the seed?
But he, the self-born one, filled with great wonder, took refuge in the lotus; through time and intense austerity, his being became purified,
O Lord, and he perceived you within himself like an exceedingly subtle fragrance upon the earth.
He beheld [the Lord] spread out within that which consists of the elements, senses, and the internal seat (āśaya), endowed with a thousand faces, feet, heads, hands, thighs,
noses, mouths, ears, eyes, ornaments, and weapons.
Having seen the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa), whose form was composed of Māyā yet perceived as truly existent, Viriñca attained great joy;
for to him you, indeed, appeared bearing the body of the horse-headed one (Hayaśiras).

Having slain the two exceedingly powerful enemies of the Vedas known as Madhu and Kaiṭabha, You brought forth the collections of the Śrutis; they declare that the quality of goodness (sattva) is Your most beloved form.
In this manner, through Your incarnations as man, animal, sage, god, and fish, You manifest the worlds, destroy those who oppose the universe,
and protect the dharma that persists throughout the ages, O Mahāpuruṣa.
O Lord of Kuṇṭha, you who became the three-yoked one (Trivikrama) hidden in the Kali age— you are indeed that very person.
Yet this mind of mine, corrupted by sin, wicked, and fierce, does not find delight in your stories.
Afflicted by lust and tormented by joy, grief, fear, and desire,
how can I, being so wretched, contemplate Your path? O Acyuta, on one side my insatiable tongue drags me away.
The penis is drawn from one direction, the skin and belly from another, the ears from yet another,
the nose from elsewhere, and the fickle eye and the power of action from somewhere else;
like many co-wives, they all tear at the master of the house.
Thus, seeing people fallen into the Vaitaraṇī river of worldly existence by their own karma—
terrified by the mutual cycle of birth, death, and devouring one another, and characterized by hostility or friendship toward their own or others' bodies— [he remained indifferent].

"Alas! O wanderer to the further shore, protect this fool today. O Blessed One, teacher of all, what effort indeed is required for you here in the rescue of this one, who is the cause for the destruction of the cycle of worldly existence?"
O friend of the distressed, this great favor toward the foolish is indeed for us who serve Your beloved ones;
we do not tremble at the Vaitaraṇī river, which is so difficult for others to cross.
My mind is immersed in the great nectar of singing Your heroic deeds; therefore,
I grieve for those deluded ones whose minds are turned away from You, who carry the burden of sense objects for the sake of illusory pleasure.
O Lord, for the most part, sages desiring their own liberation practice silence in solitude, not being intent on the welfare of others;
yet you alone, desiring to liberate them, do not abandon these wretched ones.
I perceive no other refuge for this wandering soul but You;
for the happiness of householders derived from sexual union and the like is indeed trivial, resulting only in misery after misery, like scratching with one's own hands.
The miserable ones here, who partake in manifold sufferings, find no satisfaction;
rather, a wise person should endure the god of love as one endures an itch.
[This is achieved through] the vow of silence, sacred learning, austerity, study, and one's own duty.
O Supreme Person, for those who have not conquered their senses, as well as for the hypocritical, exposition, recitation, and meditative absorption— which lead to liberation—
become mere idle talk, or perhaps they do not even amount to that here.

These two forms of yours, existence and non-existence, created by the Veda, are like a seed and its sprout; for You who are formless, no other [cause] is possible, yet those with vision perceive You present in both.
Through yoga, You may be perceived as fire within wood, but not otherwise;
You are air, fire, earth, ether, and water— the subtle elements (mātrās)—
as well as the vital breaths, the senses, the heart, and the grace of consciousness.
O Infinite One, You alone are everything—both possessed of qualities and devoid of qualities;
there is nothing else that can be described by mind or speech apart from You.
These qualities, as well as those who possess them, such as Mahat and the rest, do not exist independently of You.
O You of vast strides, all things beginning with the mind and including mortal beings, being subject to birth and death, truly know You;
having reflected thus, the wise desist from the pursuit of words.

O most worthy of honor, what need is there for prostrations, hymns of praise, ritual worship, service at your feet, remembrance, or listening to your stories, when all these six limbs of devotion are fulfilled simply through service unto you?
"May people attain devotion toward Him who has attained the state of the Paramahaṃsas.
Śrī Nārada said:
"Thus have the qualities of the one beyond all attributes been described by the devotee through his devotion."
Pleased with Prahlāda as he bowed down, the Lord, his anger subsided, spoke to him.
The Blessed One said:
"O Prahlāda, may there be welfare for you, O auspicious one! I am pleased with you, O best of Asuras."
"Choose a boon that you desire; I am the fulfiller of the wishes of men.
O long-lived one, my sight is difficult to obtain for those who do not please me. Having seen me, a living being ought never again to suffer for his own self."
"For the wise and saintly, O fortunate one, desiring the highest good, please me with their whole being, as I am the lord of all blessings. Śrī Nārada said:
Although he was thus enticed with boons that allure the world,
that best of demons, due to his single-minded devotion to the Blessed Lord, did not desire them.
Śrī Nārada said:
Considering all of that to be an obstacle to the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*),
the child Hṛṣīkeśa, smiling, spoke. Śrī Prahlāda said:
"Do not entice me with those boons, for I am attached to desires through their production;
fearing attachment to them, I have become disillusioned and, seeking liberation, have taken refuge in you.
Desiring to know the characteristics of a servant, you did not urge me toward desires, though I am your devotee."
O Lord, O Teacher of all, O Compassionate One, it is not otherwise possible for you that the knots of the heart— the seeds of worldly existence— should remain;
for he who seeks blessings from you is neither a servant nor a true devotee, but merely a merchant.
A servant certainly does not desire blessings for himself from his master,
nor does a master, desiring lordship, bestow blessings upon his servant.
But I am your devotee without any other desire, and you are my master who has no one else to rely upon.

"Otherwise, there is no purpose for us two here, like that of two royal servants. O best of givers of boons, if you will grant me my desires, then I choose as my boon this: that your desires never take root in my heart."
The senses, the mind, the vital breath, the self, virtue, fortitude, intelligence,
modesty, prosperity, splendor, memory, and truth— all these perish with the birth of one for whom [the Lord] has departed.
When a human being renounces the desires residing in the mind, [he attains liberation].
At that very moment, O lotus-eyed one, he became fit for the state of the Blessed Lord:
"Om, obeisances unto You, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, the Great Soul,
Hari, the wondrous Lion, Brahman, the Supreme Self."
The Blessed Lord said:
"Those like you, who are my exclusive devotees, never desire any blessings from me, whether in this world or in the next.
Nevertheless, enjoy here for the duration of this Manvantara the pleasures belonging to the lords of the Daityas."

Delighting in my dear narrations, having absorbed Me—the one who dwells within the self—into your own being, worship Me, the Lord, as the presiding deity of sacrifice in all beings, while impelling your actions through yoga.
Then, by means of experience, cast off merit; by skillful means, cast off sin; and by the force of time, cast off this body.
Having spread your pure fame, which is sung in the world of the gods, you shall come to me with your bonds released. That man who recites this which has been sung by you to me,
remembering both you and me at the time of death, is liberated from the bondage of karma.
Śrī Prahlāda said:
"O Maheśvara, O giver of boons, choose a boon from me;
for my father, being ignorant of Your divine majesty, has censured You."
With his heart pierced by indignation, holding the false view that the Lord— the direct teacher of all the worlds— is merely my brother, and being full of sin toward You and Your devotee,
may my father be purified from that evil which is difficult to cross and hard to endure.
"O you who are compassionate toward the wretched, you have been purified by my side-long glance.
Then the Blessed Lord said:
"O sinless one, your father has been purified, along with twenty-one generations of his ancestors."

O virtuous one, since you were born in this family, you are indeed the purifier of the lineage. Wherever there are saintly devotees of Mine— tranquil, impartial in vision, and of noble conduct— even those lands are purified, even if they be the Kīkaṭas.

O Lord of the Daityas, those men in this world who follow you as my devotees do not, with their whole being, cause injury to any living creature, whether high or low, for they have lost all desire through absorption in me.
"You are indeed the embodiment of all my devotees.
Perform in every way the funeral rites for my purified father;
by the touch of my body, O dear one, he shall go to the higher worlds along with his virtuous offspring."
"O dear one, occupy your paternal station as prescribed by the exponents of the Veda; fixing your mind upon Me, perform your duties with Me as your supreme goal.
Śrī Nārada said:
Prahlāda also performed for his father those funeral rites which were appropriate for the deceased;
O King, he was consecrated by the twice-born as directed by the Blessed One,
and he beheld Brahmā, Narahari, and Hari with their faces graced by favor.
Having praised him with pure words, surrounded by the gods and others, he spoke.
Śrī Brahmā said:
"O God of gods, sovereign of all, creator of beings, first-born!"
"By good fortune, that wicked asura who tormented the world has been slain by you—
he who, having obtained a boon from me, was not to be killed by any of my created beings, and who,
emboldened by the power of his asceticism and yoga, destroyed all the Vedas."

"By good fortune, your virtuous son, that great devotee in his childhood, has been liberated from death by you; by good fortune, he has now been reunited with you. O Blessed One, this is your very form as you were meditating upon the Supreme Self."
[O Lord], you are the protector from all fears, even from death that seeks to destroy. The Blessed Lord said: "O All-pervading One, O Lotus-born, this [weapon] must not be given to the Asuras."
"A boon to those of cruel nature is like nectar to serpents.
Śrī Nārada said:
"O King, having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Hari then vanished from that place."
Invisible to all beings, he was honored by the Supreme Lord (Brahmā).
Then, having worshipped him, Prahlāda bowed his head to the Supreme Lord; likewise, he paid homage to Bhava, the Prajāpatis, and the gods, who are all portions of the Blessed Lord.
Then, together with Kāvya and other sages, the Lotus-seated Lord (Brahmā) appointed Prahlāda as the sovereign of the Daityas and Dānavas.
Thereupon, the gods, having offered their greetings, bestowed upon him the highest blessings.
O King, Brahmā and the others, having been duly honored, returned to their own abodes.
Thus, the two attendants of Viṣṇu were brought to the state of being Diti’s sons,
and were slain by Hari, who resided within their hearts in the form of enmity.
Furthermore, due to the curse of a brahmin, those two became Rākṣasas—
Kumbhakarṇa and Daśagrīva— who were slain by the prowess of Rāma while lying on the battlefield with their hearts pierced by Rāma’s arrows.
With their minds fixed on Him, they abandoned their bodies just as they had in their previous birth; now,
born here again as Śiśupāla and Karūṣaja,
they met their end through their persistent enmity toward Hari while You were looking on.
Whatever sin they had committed previously, those kings who were enemies of Kṛṣṇa abandoned it at the end, having become one with Him, just as a caterpillar becomes a silk-worm.
To whatever extent they were distinguished by supreme devotion to the Blessed One, [to that same extent did their sins vanish].
And kings such as Śiśupāla attained identity with Hari through constant contemplation of Him.
All this that you asked me has been related to you,
including how even the enemies, such as the son of Damaghoṣa, attained identity with Hari.

This is the meritorious account of the incarnations of the high-souled Kṛṣṇa, the God who is the friend of Brahman, in which the slaying of the two primordial Daityas and the life-story of Prahlāda, the great devotee of the Lord, are told.
Devotion, knowledge, detachment, and the true nature of this Lord Hari; the description of the qualities and activities of the Lord who governs creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
and the great transformation over time of the higher and lower abodes—[all these are described here].
In this narrative, the dharma of the devotees of the Lord and the Lord Himself by whom that dharma is attained have been fully recounted, along with all matters pertaining to the supreme self;
whoever hears this meritorious narrative, which is augmented by the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu—
Having heard this with faith, one who recites it is liberated from the bonds of karma.
He who, being self-restrained, reads this account of the sport of the Lion by the Primeval Person, which includes the slaughter of the leaders of the hosts of Daityas, [is likewise freed].

Having heard of the holy majesty of the son of the Daityas, who is the foremost among the virtuous, one attains a state of fearlessness from all quarters. Indeed, you in the world of men are most fortunate; for you are sages who approach this world purifying it.

He who dwells in their homes is the Supreme Brahman itself, hidden yet manifest in human form. Indeed, he is the Great Brahman, the seeker of whom is the experience of the bliss of absolute liberation (kaivalya-nirvāṇa).
He is truly your beloved, your friend, your maternal cousin, your worthy self, the ordainer of rites, and your guru.

May this Lord of the Sātvatas be gracious to me—He whose true form has not been described as a reality by even Brahmā, the lotus-born, and others through their intellect; yet who is worshipped through silence, devotion, and tranquility.
O King, it was that very Blessed One who spread his fame throughout the world.
Formerly, by Maya, the master of infinite illusions, [the sacrifice] of the god Rudra was destroyed.
The King said:
"In what ritual did Maya slay the god who is the Lord of the Universe?"
"And let it be told how fame was accumulated by this Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Nārada said:
"The Asuras were conquered by the gods when they were supported in battle by him."
They sought refuge with Maya, the supreme teacher of illusionists. The all-pervading Lord, having fashioned three cities— of gold, silver, and iron—
made them such that their destruction and conjunction were difficult to perceive, and their constituent parts were inconceivable.

O King, those commanders of the asura armies, remembering their former enmity, destroyed the three worlds along with their presiding lords while remaining unobserved. Then those worlds, together with their lords, approached the Supreme Lord and bowed down before Him.
"O Lord, protect us, Your devotees, who have been destroyed by the inhabitants of Tripura!
Then the omnipresent Blessed One, showing favor to the gods, said, "Do not fear," and fixing an arrow upon His bow, He discharged the weapon at the cities.

Then, arrows the color of fire shot forth from the solar disc like a mass of rays; because of them, none could be seen ahead. Struck by those arrows, all the inhabitants of the city fell down lifeless.
Having brought them there, the great yogi Maya cast them into the liquid of the *kūpa* well;
touched by the essence of perfected nectar, those beings of immense power rose up like lightning-flashes from a cloud, as hard as adamant.
Seeing the bull-bannered god Śiva dejected and frustrated in his resolve,
Lord Viṣṇu then devised a stratagem there:
at that time, Brahmā became the calf and this very Viṣṇu himself became the cow.
Having entered Tripura at that time, he drank the nectar from the well of rasa;
even though those asuras saw him, they did not stop him, being utterly deluded. Perceiving this, the great yogi spoke thus to the guardians of the nectar:
Smiling, free from sorrow, and remembering that divine course of events which afflicts those who are already stricken by grief, he thought:
"Whether it be a god, an asura, a human, or anyone else, there is no one here who is the Lord; for the destiny of both oneself and another cannot be overturned by anyone through divine power."
Then, with his own powers consisting of virtue, knowledge, dispassion, prosperity, austerity, learning, and ritual action, he fashioned for Śambhu a chariot,
a charioteer, a banner, steeds, a bow, armor, arrows, and all else that was required.
Having girded himself and mounted his chariot, the Lord took up his bow and an arrow;
having fixed the arrow upon the bow during the moment of the *abhijit* constellation,
O King, Hara then consumed the three cities, which were otherwise impenetrable.
In the heavens, hundreds of celestial chariots crowded together, and the kettledrums resounded;
the divine sages, ancestors, perfected beings, and lords, shouting "Victory!", showered down heaps of flowers,
while throngs of Apsarases sang and danced in joy.
O King, having thus burnt the three cities, the Blessed One,
the destroyer of the cities, being praised by Brahmā and the other gods, returned to His own abode.
Such are the deeds of this Hari, who, through His own *māyā*, imitates the ways of the human world.
What more shall I say? I shall now recount the heroic deeds sung by the seers, which purify the world, of the Teacher of the Universe.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard the well-spoken words of the foremost among the great souls, who were honored by the assembly, regarding the Self of the Wide-Striding One (Urukrama)...
Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with joy, again questioned the son of the Lord of the Daityas, the son of the Self-born.
Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear the eternal dharma of human beings."
O Brahmin, you who are endowed with the conduct of the social classes and stages of life, that which a person attains as supreme,
you have indeed obtained; for you are the direct son of Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati, and among his sons, O Brahmin, you are the most esteemed on account of your austerity, yoga, and meditative absorption.
"O Brahmins devoted to Nārāyaṇa, you who are compassionate, virtuous, and peaceful, know the supreme and secret dharma; others like them do not.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having bowed down to the Blessed One, the Unborn, the bridge of dharma for the worlds,
I shall proclaim the eternal dharma heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa— He who descended by His own portion through lawful means into the womb of the daughter of Dakṣa.
For the welfare of the worlds, the Blessed Lord Hari— who is the root of dharma and consists of all the Vedas— resides at the Badarikāśrama performing austerities; and this,
O King, is remembered by those who know Him, whereby the self becomes serene.
Truthfulness, compassion, austerity, purity, forbearance, discernment, tranquility, self-control,
non-violence, celibacy, renunciation, study of the Vedas, and straightforwardness;
contentment, equanimity, service [to the guru], and the gradual withdrawal from worldly pleasures.
For men, the vision of the reversal [of worldly existence], silence, self-inquiry,
the distribution of food and other necessities to all beings according to their merit,
and the perception of the Self and the Deity within them— especially among human beings, O Pāṇḍava— are the means.

Hearing and chanting about Him, remembering His ways, serving the great souls who have attained Him, worshiping Him, bowing down before Him, serving as His servant, befriending Him, and surrendering one’s very self—
this is declared to be the supreme duty for all human beings.

O King, he who possesses the thirty characteristics and by whom the Self of all is pleased—he is a twice-born man whose purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are uninterrupted; such a person is one whom the Unborn One has declared to be a *dvija*. Sacrifice, study, and charity are ordained for the twice-born.

The duties prescribed for the stages of life (āśrama) for those purified by their birth and karma include, for a Brahmin, the six duties beginning with Vedic study; for others, the non-acceptance of gifts;
and for a king who protects his subjects, his livelihood may be through taxes and the like from those other than Brahmins.
The Vaiśya, however, should have agriculture and trade as his livelihood, always following the path of the Brahminical community.

The Śūdra’s livelihood should consist of service to the twice-born and attendance upon his master. Agriculture is manifold; it includes the livelihood of the settled householder (śālīna), the wandering mendicant (yāyāvara), and the gathering of gleaned grains (śiloñchana).
This fourfold mode of livelihood (vṛtti) becomes increasingly superior in each successive stage.

A man should not, except in times of distress, resort to a lower mode of livelihood when a higher one is available; however, this restriction does not apply to the Kṣatriya in times of emergency, for all classes may adopt any means whatsoever when in dire straits.
One should live by means of *ṛta*, *amṛta*, *mṛta*, or *pramṛta*, or even by *satyānṛta*; one should never live by the "dog's livelihood" (*śvavṛtti*).
*Ṛta* is said to be gathering grains with a sieve (*uñcha-śila*), and *amṛta* is that which is obtained unasked.
Constant begging is called "death," while agriculture is known as "living death. Trade is "truth-and-falsehood," and serving the low-born is the "dog's livelihood.
A Brahmin and a Kṣatriya should always avoid that despised way of life.
The Brahmin consists of all the Vedas; the King consists of all the gods.
Tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, purity, contentment, forbearance, uprightness, knowledge, compassion, devotion to Acyuta, and truthfulness are the characteristics of a Brahmin.
Valor, heroism, fortitude, splendor, renunciation, self-mastery, forgiveness,

devotion to the Brahmanas, serenity, and truthfulness are the characteristics of the Kṣatriya. Devotion to the gods, the guru, and Acyuta, as well as the cultivation of the three aims of life (trivarga), [are also his duties].
Faith in the scriptures, constant exertion, and skillfulness are the characteristics of a Vaiśya. For a Śūdra, the characteristics are humility, purity, and service to his master without guile;
for he has no sacrificial mantras, yet he must practice non-stealing, truthfulness, and the protection of cows and Brahmins.

For women whose deity is their husband, there is the practice of serving him, acting in accordance with his will, constant devotion toward his kinsmen, and the perpetual observance of his vows; [this is achieved] through sweeping, smearing [the floor], and the constant beautification of the home.
Adorning herself constantly and keeping her garments polished,
the virtuous wife should serve her husband at the proper times with various desires, with humility and self-restraint, and with truthful, pleasing words out of love.
Contented, free from greed, skillful, knowing the dharma, speaking kind and truthful words,
vigilant, pure, and affectionate— a wife should serve her husband so long as he has not fallen from his status.
She who serves her husband with the same devotion as she would the Lord Hari, being entirely dedicated to him, is like the goddess Śrī herself.
With Hari as her soul, she rejoices in the world of Hari like Śrī with her Lord.
The livelihood of those born of mixed castes, who are neither thieves nor sinful, shall be determined by their respective families, even if they are outcasts or dwellers on the fringes of society.

O King, the dharma ordained by nature for human beings in each successive age has been recorded by those who perceive the Vedas; it brings about well-being both in this world and after death. One who performs one's own duties while subsisting by the livelihood prescribed by one's nature [attains this].
By gradually abandoning actions born of one's own nature, one attains freedom from the modes of material nature;
just as a field that is repeatedly plowed becomes naturally devoid of its former vigor,
it is no longer fit for further cultivation and the seed sown therein perishes.

O King, by thus excessively indulging in sensual desires, the mind whose nature is desire becomes dispassionate toward them, just as fire is extinguished by drops of water. Whatever characteristic has been declared for a man as indicative of his specific social class (varṇa), [that too is subject to change].
Whatever else might be seen elsewhere, that one should point out by means of that very [text].
Śrī Nārada said:
A celibate student, living in the teacher’s household, self-controlled, and intent on the welfare of the guru...
Behaving like a servant and remaining humble toward his guru with firm affection,
he should worship the guru, the fire, the sun, and the supreme deities in the evening and the morning;
and at both twilights, with speech restrained and mind concentrated, he should chant the sacred Veda.

When summoned by his guru, he should study the Vedic meters while remaining well-restrained; at both the beginning and the conclusion, he should bow with his head to the guru's feet. He should wear a girdle, a deerskin garment, matted hair, a staff, and a water-pot.
He should wear the sacred thread and hold *darbha* grass in his hand as prescribed.
He should go for alms in the evening and morning and offer it to his guru;
if permitted by him, he may eat, otherwise he should fast at times.
Virtuous, moderate in eating, skillful, full of faith, and having conquered his senses,
he should engage with women and those conquered by women only as much as is necessary. One who has not yet entered the householder stage and observes the great vow should avoid songs about women.
The turbulent senses carry away even the mind of an ascetic; therefore,
while still young, he should have his hair combed, massaged, bathed, and anointed by elderly women and not by young ones.

Indeed, a woman is like fire and a man is like a jar of clarified butter; even toward his own daughter, a man might abandon her in secret at other times, acting only for his own purpose as long as he has not yet fulfilled it.
Having fashioned this world as a mere appearance by himself, the Lord [acts accordingly].
Duality shall not cease until then, for from it comes his perversion.
All this has been prescribed for the householder and also for the ascetic; however, the service of the guru is optional for the householder who approaches his wife during her season.

Those who observe the great vow (bṛhadvrata) should renounce the application of collyrium, ointments, and massage; women, scratching with fingernails, meat, and honey; as well as garlands, perfumes, unguents, and ornaments.
Having thus resided in the teacher’s household, the twice-born student, having studied and understood [the scriptures], [should depart].
Having studied the three Vedas along with their auxiliary branches and the Upaniṣads to the full extent of their meaning and according to his capacity,
and having been granted permission by his guru to choose a boon— if he so desires—
he may enter the householder’s life, retire to the forest, or remain there [in the stage of the student].
One should perceive Adhokṣaja within the fire, the guru, oneself, and in all living beings— by means of the elements and their respective abodes— as both unentered and yet entered.
Such a person, whether a student, forest-dweller, renunciant, or householder, is truly one who knows.
Practicing this, one who has realized true knowledge attains the Supreme Brahman.
I shall now describe the observances for the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) as approved by the sages;
by adhering to these, a sage may swiftly go to the exalted world of the seers.

One should not eat grain ripened by cultivation, nor that which is uncultivated but harvested out of season; one may, however, bring forth food cooked by fire, or even raw, or ripened by the sun. One should offer oblations of sacrificial pap and cakes made from wild grains as prompted by the proper time.

When new and fresh food is obtained, one should discard that which is old. For the sake of the sacred fire alone, one should take refuge in a hut or a mountain cave, personally enduring cold, wind, fire, rain, and the heat of the sun.
Wearing his hair, body hair, nails, and beard unshorn,
and bearing a water-pot, a deerskin, a staff, bark garments, fire, and other requisites,
the sage should dwell in the forest for twelve, eight, or four years.
Two or even one [of these] should be performed so that the intellect does not falter due to hardship; when one is incapable of one's own duties due to disease or old age,
or in the pursuit of philosophical knowledge (*ānvīkṣikī*), one may practice fasting and other such austerities.
Having internalized the sacred fires within himself and renounced the sense of "I" and "mine," he should properly dissolve the aggregate of the body into its constituent causes as is appropriate:
the openings of the senses into space, the breaths into the wind, and the subtle heat into fire. Thus the self-possessed one proceeds.
In the waters [he places] blood, phlegm, and pus; the remainder [of his body] according to its origin in the earth;
speech along with that which is to be spoken in Agni; craftsmanship and the hands in Indra;
the feet together with the power of movement in Vāyu; and the generative organ together with sexual pleasure in Prajāpati.
One should assign the anus for excretion to death, each according to its proper place;
the ears, along with sound, to the quarters; and the skin, through touch, to the inner self.
O King, one should dissolve forms into the eyes and light into the eyes as well.
One should place the tongue among the waters with the Pracetasas, the sense of smell among fragrances on the earth,

the mind among mental desires in the moon, and the intellect among objects of knowledge in the supreme Kavi (Brahmā). One should place ritual actions along with the ego-sense in Rudra, as well as all activities involving the notions of "I" and "mine."
By means of *sattva*, the mind is merged into the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*); by means of the qualities (*guṇas*), the modified nature (*vaikārika*) is merged into the Supreme.
Earth is merged into water, water into fire, fire into air, and that air into space;
that space is merged into the immutable (*kūṭastha*), and that into the Great Principle (*mahat*), and that into the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), and that into the Imperishable (*akṣara*).

Having thus realized the Self as the non-dual, consisting of pure consciousness alone, with all else remaining as nothing but the imperishable, one should then desist from activity like a fire whose fuel has been consumed. Śrī Nārada said:

Having thus wandered as a mendicant for a kalpa, with nothing remaining but his body, he should roam the earth indifferent to all, according to the rule of staying only one night in a village; if he should wear clothing at all, it should be no more than a loincloth.
Except in times of distress, he should not discard anything other than his external marks, such as the staff;
the mendicant should wander alone, delighting in the Self, without dependence on others,
a friend to all beings, peaceful, and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
One should perceive this entire universe within the Self, which is the supreme, imperishable reality consisting of both being and non-being;
and one should perceive the Self as the Supreme Brahman everywhere, within that which is composed of both being and non-being.
One who perceives the Self beholds the movement of the Self during the transition between sleep and waking.
Seeing both bondage and liberation as mere illusion and not as reality,
he should not long for certain death nor for his uncertain life; rather,
he should await the supreme Time, which is the source and the dissolution of all beings.

One should not become attached to false scriptures, nor should one make a livelihood from them. One should abandon contentious debates and logical speculations, and should not take recourse in any partisan position. One should not bind oneself to disciples, nor should one study many books.
One should not employ oneself in explaining [scriptures], nor should one undertake any worldly undertakings anywhere.
For a great-souled ascetic who is peaceful and even-minded, the stage of life (āśrama) is generally not the cause of dharma; he may either maintain it or abandon it.

With unmanifested external signs yet manifesting his true purpose, he, a wise sage, should show himself to men like one who is insane, a child, or mute; with such a vision, he should present himself to people.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history.
And [he heard] the dialogue between Prahlāda and the sage Ājagara,
who was lying upon the surface of the earth on a ridge of the Sahya mountains by the Kāverī river,
his pure luster concealed by the dust-covered parts of his body.
Desiring to know the true nature of the worlds, Prahlāda, the beloved of the Blessed One, wandered through the worlds surrounded by a few ministers, observing people through their actions,
appearances, speech, characteristics, and their castes and stages of life.
People do not know him, thinking "this is he" or "this is not he.
Having bowed to him and worshipped him according to the rules, touching his feet with his head,
that great devotee of the Lord, the asura, desiring to know, asked this:
You bear a corpulent body, just like one who is industrious and possesses enjoyments;
for in this world, wealth belongs to those who exert effort, enjoyment belongs to those who possess wealth,
and indeed, the body of one who enjoys becomes fat— not otherwise.

"O Brahmin, you who lie down and make no effort, what purpose indeed do you have from which this enjoyment arises? O sage, tell us if it pleases you how it is that this body of yours is fat despite your lack of enjoyment; for you are a wise man, capable, keen-sighted, a narrator of wonderful and pleasing stories, and equanimous."
"While the world was performing its ritual duties, you remained there as its witness.
Śrī Nārada said:
"Thus questioned by the lord of the Daityas, the great sage—"
Smiling, and constrained by the nectar of his words, he spoke to him;
the illustrious brāhmaṇa said:
"O best of asuras, you are surely esteemed by the noble ones; you know this from the Vedas."
With the eye of spiritual insight, one perceives the stations of men regarding worldly involvement and renunciation;
for him in whose heart the Lord Nārāyaṇa ever resides,
pure devotion dispels ignorance just as the sun dispels darkness.
Nevertheless, O King, I shall answer your questions according to what I have heard;
for you are worthy of being conversed with by one who desires the purification of the self.
[Yet] you are driven by the thirst that carries one through worldly existence, which is never satisfied even by appropriate objects of desire.
While performing various actions, I have been joined to diverse wombs; wandering through the cycle of karma, I have by chance arrived at this world,
which is the gateway to heaven, liberation, the state of animals, and even rebirth.
Even there, seeing that couples perform rituals for the sake of their own pleasure and the removal of other afflictions— this being a reversal of the truth— I have desisted;
for happiness is the very nature of the self, while the body is merely the cessation of all worldly engagement.
"Having seen the enjoyments born of mental contact, I shall sleep while lying down"—
forgetting this true purpose of the self, a person indeed undergoes the terrible cycle of worldly existence, which is manifold despite the non-existence of duality.

Just as an ignorant man, seeing water covered by its own products, abandons it and runs toward a mirage out of a desire for water, so too does one who perceives objects elsewhere seek his own happiness through the body and other instruments that are dependent on destiny.
For one who is powerless, actions performed repeatedly are in vain;
for a mortal who is never liberated from the sufferings of the self and other realms, what can be achieved by objects of desire acquired through great hardship?
I behold the suffering of the wealthy who are greedy and have no self-control—
those who, out of fear, find no sleep and are suspicious of everything on every side:
of the king, of thieves, of enemies, of their own kin, and even of beasts and birds.

A wise person should abandon the desire for life and wealth, which are like fear to those who seek them at the proper time; for from these arise in men grief, delusion, fear, anger, passion, impotence, fatigue, and other such states.
In this world, the honeybee and the great serpent are our two most excellent gurus;
through their instruction, we have attained detachment and contentment.
From the honeybee, I learned detachment from all desires.
Wealth acquired through hardship may be seized by another even after killing its owner, like honey;
therefore, being free from worldly effort and content in soul, I shall subsist on whatever comes by chance.
Otherwise, I shall lie down like a powerful great serpent, enduring many days of fasting.

In one place I eat little, in another much; sometimes the food is tasty, sometimes tasteless; sometimes it is abundant and endowed with excellent qualities, and at other times it is devoid of them; in some instances it is offered with faith, and at others it is bereft of respect.
Having eaten, I eat again at some time by chance, whether by day or by night.
I wear linen, fine silk, deerskin, rags, or even bark garments;
whatever else comes to me, I am content in mind, eating only what is ordained by destiny.
Sometimes he lies on the bare ground, on grass, leaves, stones, or ashes;
sometimes, by the will of another, he rests upon a palace couch or a soft bed.
At other times, he is bathed, his limbs anointed with unguents, well-dressed, wearing garlands, and adorned with ornaments.
O Lord, sometimes You wander about naked like a madman on chariots, elephants, and horses;
I neither censure nor praise people who are so diverse by nature. I pray only for their ultimate welfare, or rather, for their identity with the Great Self.
One should offer conceptualization into the mind, that mind into the fluctuation of objects;
having offered the mind into the ego (vaikārika), one should subsequently offer that into Māyā.
The sage who perceives the Truth should offer that Māyā into the self-realization of the Self.
Therefore, free from desire and established in the Self through self-realization, one should desist from worldly activity.
Thus have I described to you my own spiritual practice, though it is well-guarded;
for you are devoted solely to the Blessed Lord, being beyond both worldly custom and the dictates of the scriptures.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King of the Asuras, having heard the dharma of the paramahaṃsas from the sage, the lord was pleased;
he honored him, took his leave, and departed for his home.
Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O divine sage, please tell me how a householder like me, whose intellect is deluded by domestic life, may easily attain this path according to the prescribed injunctions.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, remaining in his home and performing his duties as is appropriate,
he should directly worship the great sages by offering everything to Vāsudeva.
Constantly hearing the nectar of the stories of the Lord’s incarnations,
full of faith, and surrounded by peaceful people at the appropriate times,
he gradually [severs] his attachment to wife, children, and other kin through the company of the virtuous.

When those who are being liberated are released, the wise man, having awakened from his own dream-like state, should withdraw himself. Remaining in his body and home only as much as necessary, detached though appearing attached, he should establish his human nature in this world of men.
One who is free from the sense of "mine" should approve whatever his kinsmen, parents, sons, brothers, friends, and others say or desire;
for wealth— whether celestial, terrestrial, or atmospheric— is created by Acyuta.
Utilizing all that for his own needs, the wise man should act in this manner;
for as long as the belly is filled, so far extends the ownership of embodied beings.
He who considers himself the owner of more than that is a thief and deserves punishment.

One should look upon deer, camels, donkeys, horses, rats, reptiles, birds, and flies as one’s own children; what difference, then, could there be between them? Even a householder may pursue the three aims of life (trivarga) without excessive hardship.
According to place and time,
one should distribute as much as is provided by fate among those who are dependent and desiring relief,
even if it be only a single wife, since men possess a sense of ownership over her.

One should abandon that woman for whose sake one would sacrifice one's own life or kill a father or a guru; for by him who has conquered her, he is truly conquered. Where is this wretched body, which ends as worms, excrement, or ashes?

Where is his wife, who is so devoted to him, and where is this self of his that covers the sky? With the remnants of the sacrifice, a wise man should provide for his own livelihood; by relinquishing ownership over what remains, he shall follow the path of the great.

Every day, one should worship the gods, the sages, human beings, the ancestors, and the Self with wealth acquired through one’s own prescribed occupation, offering it individually to the Supreme Person. For when all these elements of sacrifice are present, they constitute the complete perfection of one’s own duty.
One should worship with the ritual of the three sacred fires, such as the *agnihotra* and others;

for this Blessed One, the enjoyer of all sacrifices, is indeed not worshipped by means of oblations poured into the mouth of the fire, O King, in the same way as he is worshipped by offerings poured into the mouth of a Brahmin.

Therefore, among the Brahmanas, the gods, and mortals, worship this Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) with various desired objects as is appropriate, following the guidance of the Brahmanas. In the month of Prauṣṭhapada, the twice-born man should perform the rites belonging to the dark fortnight.

One who possesses wealth should perform the *śrāddha* for his parents and their relatives according to his means during the solstices (*ayana*), the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), the *vyatīpāta* yoga, the *dinakṣaya*,
during eclipses of the moon or sun, on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*), and under the asterism of Śravaṇa.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, on the ninth day as well,
during the four Aṣṭakās of both Hemanta and Śiśira,
and on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha when the moon is in conjunction with the Maghā constellation;
The lunar mansions conjoined with the lunar days of Rākā and Anumati; on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) there was Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, and the three Uttaras;
and on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) among those three, there was the conjunction of his birth-mansion with Śroṇā.
These times are conducive to the highest good for men and increase their spiritual welfare. During these periods, one should devote oneself entirely to that which makes the life-span fruitful;
therein, bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, vows, and the worship of the gods and the twice-born [are to be performed].
O King, that which is given to the ancestors, the gods, men, and living beings is indeed imperishable; likewise, the time for the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) of one's wife, offspring, and oneself,
as well as the funeral ceremonies (pretasaṃsthā), the anniversary of death (mṛtāha), and rites for prosperity (abhyudaya).
Now I shall describe those regions which bring about the highest good, such as dharma and other virtues.
That indeed is the most meritorious region where a worthy recipient (sat-pātra) is found;
and wherever there is an image of the Blessed One, all this world of moving and non-moving beings is present there.
Wherever there is a family of Brahmins endowed with austerity, knowledge, and compassion;
wherever there is an image of Hari; and wherever there are rivers such as the Gaṅgā renowned in the Purāṇas—that place is the abode of all auspicious things.
The lakes such as Puṣkara and others, as well as the sacred sites inhabited by the Arhats;
Kurukṣetra, Gayaśiras, Prayāga, Pulahāśrama,
Naimiṣa, Phālguna, Setu, Prabhāsa, and Kuśasthalī.
Vārāṇasī, Madhupurī, Pampā, and likewise Bindusaras;
Nārāyaṇāśrama, Nandā, Sītārāmāśrama, and others;
and all the principal mountain ranges, O King, such as Mahendra, Malaya, and the rest.

These are the most sacred regions where the worship of Hari is established; one who desires his own welfare should indeed frequent these places constantly. For dharma practiced here by men yields a thousandfold increase in its fruit.

O Lord of the Earth, regarding this matter, the wise who are most proficient in the knowledge of worthy recipients have indeed declared that Hari alone is the true recipient, for the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings consists of Him.
This was said even while the sons of Brahmā and other celestial sages, who were themselves worthy of honor, were present there.

O King, since Acyuta is considered the foremost object of worship by virtue of being the worthy recipient, and since the great tree of the cosmic egg is filled with multitudes of living beings, the worship of Acyuta— which has that tree as its root— is the gratification of the self of all living beings.
In the past, he created the cities— the human, animal, ṛṣi, and divine beings—
for this Puruṣa indeed lies within those cities by means of the form of the individual soul (jīva).
O King, the Blessed Lord resides within them according to their relative gradations.
Therefore,
O King, seeing that among those men there was mutual contempt and a nature characterized by self-conceit,
the wise established the worship of the image of Hari for the sake of ritual action during the Tretā and subsequent ages, according to the capacity and nature of each individual.
Therefore, some worship Hari in an image with faith and ritual service;
yet even when worshipped, He does not grant their desired objects to those who hate the Supreme Person (puruṣadviṣ).
O King of kings, among men as well, they know the brāhmaṇa to be the most worthy recipient.
Through austerity, sacred knowledge, and contentment, one upholds the Veda, which is the body of Hari.
Indeed, O King, the brāhmaṇas of this Kṛṣṇa, the Soul of the universe, purify the three worlds with the dust of their feet; they are the supreme deity.
Śrī Nārada said:
Some twice-born ones are devoted to ritual action, others, the kings, are devoted to austerity;
some are intent on Vedic study, others on exposition, and some on knowledge and yoga.

One who desires infinite results should offer the *kavya* (ancestral offerings) to those established in knowledge; in the case of offerings to the gods (*daiva*), it should likewise be given to such persons, or in their absence, to others as is appropriate.
For rites to the gods, two [should be invited]; for rites to the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*), three; or one for each of the two groups.
Even if one is very wealthy, one should feed [the guests] and should not make the *śrāddha* ceremony overly elaborate.
Proper regard for the place and time, faith, the materials, and the worthiness of the recipients—
all these are correctly fulfilled, and not by the extensive feeding of one's own kinsmen.

When the proper place and time have arrived, food fit for sages dedicated to Lord Hari, when offered with faith according to the rules into a worthy recipient, becomes a wish-fulfilling cow that yields inexhaustible results—
for the gods, sages, ancestors, living beings, oneself, and one's own kin.

While distributing food, one should perceive all of it as being of the nature of the Supreme Person (puruṣa). One who knows the truth of dharma should not offer meat at a śrāddha ceremony, nor should he eat it; for the highest satisfaction is attained through the foods of sages, which cannot be achieved by the slaughter of animals.

For men who desire the true dharma, there is no higher duty than this: the renunciation of the staff of mind, speech, and body toward all living beings. Some, though they are the best among those who know sacrifice, are performers of sacrifices consisting of ritual action.
Those who are self-restrained and free from worldly desire offer their actions into the fire kindled by knowledge.
But seeing one about to perform sacrifices with material offerings, living beings become afraid, thinking:
"This merciless man, ignorant of the truth and greedy for life, will surely kill us."
Therefore, one who knows the dharma, being satisfied even with the food of a sage obtained by providence, should perform the obligatory and occasional rites day after day.
[False dharma] is: that which is contrary to dharma (vidharma), the dharma of others (paradharma), a mere semblance (ābhāsa), a counterfeit (upamā), and deception (chala).
One who knows the Dharma should abandon these five branches of unrighteousness as if they were vice itself:
*vidharma*, which is the subversion of Dharma; *paradharma*, which is the duty enjoined for others;
*upadharma*, which is heresy (*pākhaṇḍa*); hypocrisy (*dambha*); and deception (*chala*) under the guise of sacred words.

Indeed, for whom is that dharma not desired which is ordained by one's own nature for the sake of tranquility— a semblance created by men according to their will, distinct from the [four] stages of life?
Even a poor man should not strive for wealth, whether for the sake of religious duty or for the sake of mere subsistence.

The happiness that belongs to one who is free from desire, who is satisfied like a great serpent receiving its sustenance without effort, and who delights in his own self while devoid of worldly exertion— whence could that happiness come to one who runs in all directions, driven by lust and greed for the pursuit of wealth?
For one whose mind is always contented, all directions are filled with auspiciousness,
just as for one wearing shoes, there is well-being despite pebbles, thorns, and the like.
O King, by what means would a contented person not subsist, even if it were only water?
Out of lust for sexual pleasure, greed, and wretchedness, people act like householders;
for a dissatisfied brahmin, his splendor, learning, austerity,
and fame flow away through the restlessness of the senses, and even his knowledge is scattered.

Indeed, people reach the end of desire through hunger and thirst, and the end of anger through the arising of its fruit; yet they do not reach the end of greed, even after conquering and enjoying all the quarters of the earth.
O King, there have been many wise men, deeply learned and destroyers of doubt.
Even some who are lords of the assembly fall downward due to discontent. One should conquer desire through the absence of mental construction, anger by abandoning desire,
greed by perceiving the worthlessness of objects, and fear by reflecting upon the ultimate reality.

One should abandon grief and delusion through the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), hypocrisy by worshiping the Great One (Brahman), obstacles to yoga through silence, and violence along with desire and other impulses through lack of worldly striving;
one should abandon suffering born of living beings through compassion, and that which is caused by fate through meditative absorption (samādhi).

A person may easily conquer the son of the Self (the mind) through the power of yoga; sleep by cultivating goodness (*sattva*); passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*) by means of goodness; and goodness itself by means of tranquility. Indeed, one conquers all of this through devotion to the Guru.

The learning of one who harbors a false conception of the mortal world toward the spiritual master— who is the direct manifestation of the Lord and the bestower of the lamp of knowledge— is like the bathing of an elephant.
Indeed, this spiritual master is the Lord himself, the sovereign of both primordial nature (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa).
His feet are sought after by the masters of yoga, yet the world regards him as a mere man; all injunctions regarding observances, which consist solely in the restraint of the six internal enemies,
culminate in him— if they do not lead to yoga, they are merely a source of weariness.
Just as the pursuits of livelihood and the like do not support the purpose of yoga,

but rather lead to misfortune, so too do ritual sacrifices and charitable works lead to harm for one who is devoid of self-control. He who is intent on conquering the mind should remain free from attachment and without possessions.
O King, a mendicant who has taken refuge in solitude, eating only as much as is obtained through alms,
should establish his own seat in a clean and level place; having made it firm, comfortable, and even, he should sit upon it with his limbs straight, uttering "Om."
One should restrain the prāṇa and apāna breaths through inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka),
while gazing at the tip of one's own nose, until the mind abandons its desires.
For wherever the mind, struck by desire, wanders away, [one must restrain it].
Then, having withdrawn [the mind] from each respective object, the wise practitioner should gradually restrain it within the heart.
For the ascetic who practices in this way, the mind attains extinction after a short time through constant application, like a fire without fuel.

That mind which is unpierced by desire and other passions, whose entire fluctuations have been stilled, and which has been touched by the bliss of Brahman, shall never again arise from its state. This applies to one who, having previously departed from the home— which is the field for sowing the three aims of life— has taken up the life of renunciation.

If a mendicant should serve those by whom this body— which is not the self, is mortal, and is like excrement, worms, and ashes— is considered as one's own, then that shameless man is indeed an eater of vomit; for those most wretched of men, having made it their own, boast of it.
The abandonment of ritual duties by a householder, the abandonment of vows by a student, the service of a village by an ascetic, and the lust of the senses in a mendicant—
these are indeed the outcasts of their respective stages of life, mere mockeries of the āśramas.
One should look upon those who are deluded by the divine Māyā with compassion and disregard them.
If one were to know oneself as the Supreme, with the fire of knowledge having purified the heart,
what would that greedy person desire, or for whose sake would he nourish this body?
They say that the body is the chariot, the senses are the horses, and the mind is the reins; the lord of the senses is the driver.
The paths are the objects of the senses, the intellect is the charioteer, and the great seat is the mode of goodness (sattva) created by the Lord.
The axle is the ten vital breaths, the wheels are merit and demerit, and the rider on the chariot is the individual soul (jīva) characterized by egoism.
They declare that his bow is the *praṇava* (the sacred syllable Om), while the individual soul (*jīva*) is the arrow and the Supreme is the target.
Attachment, hatred, greed, grief, delusion, fear, pride,
arrogance, envy, deceit, violence, and malice— these are the impediments.
Passion, negligence, hunger, sleep, and other such enemies—
some of which are of the nature of *rajas* and *tamas*, while others are occasionally of the nature of *sattva—
persist as long as the chariot of the human body remains under the control of the self.
Having whetted the sword of knowledge by worshipping the feet of the Most Revered One,
and having destroyed his enemies while wielding that sword, he— content in his own bliss and fully tranquil— would cast off this world, O Acyuta, through the strength of your power.
If not, then the horses of the unwholesome senses— acting as charioteers for the negligent man— lead him astray and cast him among the robbers of sense-objects;
those robbers, together with the charioteer, hurl him into blinding darkness.

In this well of worldly existence, where the fear of death is vast, they cast down both types of Vedic action—the active (*pravṛtta*) and the renounced (*nivṛtta*). By the active path one revolves in saṃsāra; by the renounced path one attains immortality.
The Agnihotra and other rites— which involve violence, consist of material substances, are performed for specific desires, and do not grant peace;
as well as the Darśa, Pūrṇamāsa, Cāturmāsya, Paśu, and Soma sacrifices—
these constitute the *iṣṭa* known as *pravṛtta*, as well as the *huta* and *prahuta*.
*Pūrta*— consisting of the construction of temples, gardens, wells, and other such works of public utility—

is the subtle ripening of material action (*dravya*). [The path of smoke consists of] night, the waning fortnight, the southern solstice (*ayana*), the moon, the new moon day (*darśa*), and herbs and creepers.
"O Lord of the Earth, food becomes semen; this is the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna) and rebirth. Having become each [element] in succession, one is born here again and again.
A twice-born man is consecrated by the purificatory rites (saṃskāras), beginning with the impregnation ceremony and ending at the cremation ground."
They offer the sacrifices of action into the senses, which are the lamps of knowledge;
they offer the senses into the wave of the mind, and the transformative mind into speech;
they offer speech into the collection of phonemes, and that darkness into the syllable Om within the tone.
One should merge the *oṃkāra* into the *bindu*, that into the *nāda*, and that into the *prāṇa*; then that into the Great (*mahat*), and that into the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).

Fire, the sun, day, morning, the white fortnight, the waxing moon, and the sovereign *svarāṭ*—these correspond respectively to Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and the Fourth (*turya*) Self through their sequential connection.
They say this is the path of the gods (devayāna), which proceeds by appearing again and again in successive stages.
Indeed, the self-sacrificer whose mind is tranquil and who is established in the Self does not return. These two paths—the way of the ancestors and the way of the gods—were fashioned by Veda.
Even while dwelling among people, one who possesses the eye of the scripture does not become deluded.

At the beginning and at the end of all beings, You Yourself are that which is both external and internal, the higher and the lower, knowledge and the object of knowledge, speech and the object of speech, darkness and light.
For just as a reflection, though afflicted by defects, is nevertheless remembered as a real object,
so too is the sensory perception of objects constructed by the mind;
for here, among objects such as earth and the rest, there is not even a shadow of reality.
Neither is it a composite, nor a modification, nor is it separate from its parts; nor is it joined with them, for such [a composite] is false.
Since the elements possess constituent parts, they cannot exist without the subtle elements as their components;
for if the whole were unreal, the part would ultimately be non-existent as well.
As long as there is conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*), there may arise the delusion of similarity regarding an object;

just as waking and sleeping appear within a dream, so too do injunctions and prohibitions exist. Thus, there is non-duality of existence, non-duality of action, and likewise non-duality of substance for the Self.
By practicing here through his own direct experience, the sage shakes off the three states of dream.
The perception of the unity of the effect and the cause, like that of a cloth and its threads,
is called the non-duality of existence (*bhāvādvaita*), because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) lacks substantial reality.
O Pārtha, that which is the direct surrender of all actions into the Supreme Brahman through mind, speech, and body is called *kriyādvaita*.
[This applies] to one's own children, wife, sons, and others— all embodied beings.

The unity of one's own material interests and desires is called the non-duality of objects (*dravyādvaita*). O King, whatever is not forbidden for a person, by whomsoever, wherever, and from whatever source, that person should pursue those activities with that means, and not by other means, except in times of distress.

O King, a man who abides by these and other duties prescribed in the Vedas, while remaining in the household life, shall attain the same goal as he [the renunciant] if he possesses devotion to Him; just as you yourselves, O divine king, have been delivered from this multitude of calamities that are so difficult to escape through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
By serving the lotus feet of whom you, having conquered the world-elephants,
performed sacrifices; formerly, in a past great kalpa, I was a certain Gandharva named Upabarhaṇa, highly esteemed among the Gandharvas.
Handsome in form, sweet-voiced, fragrant, and pleasing to behold, he was eternally beloved by women; intoxicated and ever lustful for his own city,
once, during a divine sacrifice, the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases [arrived].
When the creators of the universe were invited to sing songs of Hari,
I, knowing that [the Lord] was there, went surrounded by women and sang;
having learned of that, the creators of the universe rebuked me with their power for that offense.
"Go quickly to the state of a Śūdra, your fortune destroyed because you have shown me contempt!
While I was born there as a servant to those who discourse on Brahman,
through the incidental practice of service, I attained the status of being the son of Brahmā."

The dharma pertaining to householders, which destroys all sins, has been described by you—the dharma by which a householder may easily attain the same path as those who have renounced worldly life. Alas, in this world of men, you are most fortunate; like sages, you approach the world purifying it.

He who dwells in their homes is the Supreme Brahman itself, hidden yet manifest in human form. Indeed, he is the Great Brahman, the seeker of whom is the experience of the bliss of absolute liberation (kaivalya-nirvāṇa).
He is truly your beloved, your friend, your maternal cousin, your worthy self, your ordainer, and your guru.

May this Lord of the Sātvatas be gracious to me—he whose true form has not been described as a reality by even Brahmā, the lotus-born, and others through their intellect; yet who is worshipped through silence, devotion, and tranquility.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard what was thus spoken by the celestial sage, O bull of the Bharatas,
he honored him with great joy, overwhelmed with love, and also honored Kṛṣṇa;
then, having taken leave of Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, the sage departed after being duly worshipped.
Having heard that Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman, Arjuna was struck with supreme wonder.
Thus have the separate lineages of the daughters of Dakṣa been proclaimed,
wherein dwell the worlds of gods, asuras, humans, and others, both moving and non-moving.
